domains.name: AI Lab: Engineering Around the Model
domains.summary: The engineering around the model: local inference economics, the agent operations loop, and the review patterns that keep agentic systems honest.

scenarios.title: The Weights Arrived
scenarios.situation: Your team downloads an open-weight 32B model and drops the weights into a folder. The founder declares the AI product 'basically done' — the model knows things, after all.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage next engineering step?
choices: Build the scaffolding around the model folder: prompt pipeline, tool definitions, memory, a sandboxed execution runtime, behavior tests, and trace inspection — then wire the loop from request to deploy.
Download a bigger model, since a more capable model automatically becomes a better product.
Fine-tune immediately on customer data to make the model 'know the product'.
Write more documentation describing what the model could theoretically do.
scenarios.why: A trained model is a file: weights, a tokenizer, a config. Everything that turns it into a product — retrieval, memory, tool use, sandboxing, evaluation, monitoring — is infrastructure you build, operate, and pay for. Ask what the folders around the model folder contain; that is where the engineering, and the failure modes, live.
scenarios.hint: If the weights folder disappeared tomorrow, which folders would still be 'the product'?

scenarios.title: The Quantization Exchange Rate
scenarios.situation: You have a workstation with 24 GB of VRAM and want to run a 70B-parameter open model locally. At full 16-bit precision the weights alone need roughly 140 GB; at 8-bit roughly 70 GB; at 4-bit roughly 35 GB plus overhead.
scenarios.prompt: Which quantization choice survives first contact with this hardware?
choices: Load the model at 4-bit precision (GGUF Q4), accept the modest fidelity loss, and keep the KV cache on a diet — it's the only tier that fits, and the exchange rate (memory for fidelity) is exactly the trade local inference exists to manage.
Run it at 8-bit and let the OS swap to RAM; paging is just slower memory.
Run it at full 16-bit precision; quantization destroys model quality anyway.
Split the model across two laptops over Wi-Fi to pool their VRAM.
scenarios.why: Quantization — storing weights at reduced precision — is what makes local inference survivable: a model that needs a datacenter at full precision fits on a workstation at 4-bit. The skill is knowing the exchange rate: what you lose in fidelity at each level, what VRAM and memory bandwidth actually bound, and when the honest answer is 'this workload belongs on an API.'
scenarios.hint: What is the actual binding constraint — parameter count, or memory capacity?

scenarios.title: Local Means Private? Not Yet.
scenarios.situation: You run an open-weight model locally, but you query it through a chat UI that phones home telemetry, and the notes you attach are synced to a vendor cloud by the desktop client.
choices: No. Privacy is a property of the whole data path, not of where the weights sit — the telemetry-phoning UI and the cloud-synced client break the privacy story even though inference is local.
Yes. The weights are on your hardware, so nothing leaves the machine.
Yes, as long as the model itself is open-weight.
No, because the model was trained on public internet data.
scenarios.why: Local inference is an economics and control decision — privacy is one motive, but it only holds if every hop of the data path is accounted for. Audit the UI, the sync layer, the plugin folder, and the network; the weights' location is necessary but not sufficient.
scenarios.hint: Follow one prompt from keyboard to answer: how many network hops does it make?

scenarios.title: The Green Dashboard
scenarios.situation: Your agent stack's eval dashboard is all green. The suite is 40 hand-written cases, judged by another LLM from the same model family, and the long-tail failure modes were never sampled.
scenarios.prompt: How should you read that dashboard?
choices: As evidence the agent passed the evals — nothing more. LLM-as-judge inherits the judge's biases, small suites miss the long tail, and a green dashboard on a bad metric manufactures confidence. The honest question is always: what would this eval miss?
As proof the agent works in production; green is green.
As a signal to delete the eval suite and trust user feedback instead.
As proof the agent needs no human review, since the judge is itself an AI.
scenarios.why: Evals test LLM behavior the way unit tests test code — which means they have exactly the same blind spots: coverage gaps, oracle bias, and the gap between the test distribution and production. Treat a green dashboard as a claim to interrogate, not a verdict to celebrate.
scenarios.hint: Who grades the grader, and what distribution did the grader see?

scenarios.title: One Model, Two Hats
scenarios.situation: Your agentic coding setup has a single model that writes code and then, in the same session, 'reviews' its own output before committing. Bugs are shipping anyway, and the reviews read like the model congratulating itself.
scenarios.prompt: What structural change fixes the review loop?
choices: Separate generation from verification structurally: a main writer optimized for momentum, a silent advisor that reviews only at defined trigger points (plan approval, stuck errors, pre-commit), specialist subagents dividing labor, and a cheap router keeping the expensive model on genuinely hard decisions.
Prompt the model harder to 'be more careful' during self-review.
Add a second identical model that also reviews everything; two approvals are better than one.
Disable the review step entirely — it was only slowing the pipeline.
scenarios.why: A model that writes and a model that checks should not be the same process wearing two hats. The writer is optimized for momentum — propose, build, move on. The verifier is optimized for suspicion — is this the right plan, is this error a dead end, what did speed skip? Running both in one undifferentiated session produces confident output with unchecked assumptions. The main-writer / silent-advisor pattern makes the separation structural: distinct roles, distinct trigger points, cheap decisions routed away from the expensive mind.
scenarios.hint: When the reviewer disagrees with the writer, who in your current setup is allowed to disagree?

scenarios.title: vLLM on the Laptop
scenarios.situation: A teammate proposes installing vLLM on everyone's laptop for local inference, arguing 'it's the best inference engine, so it must be best everywhere.'
choices: vLLM is a production serving stack for operators — batched, multi-GPU, throughput-oriented — a different discipline for a different audience. The local tier is llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, Jan, and web UIs like Open WebUI; matching the runtime tier to the job is the skill.
Nothing — the best engine is the best engine regardless of setting.
vLLM doesn't run on laptops because of licensing restrictions.
The plan is fine; laptops just need more RAM.
scenarios.why: The inference ecosystem has honest tiers: the runtime layer (llama.cpp, Ollama, LocalAI), the desktop layer (LM Studio, Jan, GPT4All), the web-UI layer (Open WebUI, text-generation-webui), and the production serving tier (vLLM) — which is for operators running fleets, not desktops. Using the wrong tier buys operational complexity without the workload that justifies it.
scenarios.hint: Who is the audience of each runtime tier — a developer's laptop, or a fleet operator?

scenarios.title: The AI Lab: Engineering Around the Model Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that AI Lab: Engineering Around the Model is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in AI Lab: Engineering Around the Model?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — AI Lab: Engineering Around the Model issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — AI Lab: Engineering Around the Model is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct approach is as follows: Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is AI Lab: Engineering Around the Model supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any AI Lab: Engineering Around the Model failure in Ai Lab.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.

scenarios.title: Navigate the Bootcamp
scenarios.situation: You have 30 days before your assessment. You open the bootcamp and see 15 domains, a terminal, drills, and a mock. You feel overwhelmed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage first week plan?
choices: Complete Start Here, then work the first three core domains in order — lessons with knowledge checks, then their scenarios, then one lab. Establish the daily loop before widening.
Take the full mock on day one to 'see where you stand,' then study randomly.
Read every lesson in all 15 domains first, then attempt scenarios in week three.
Skip lessons entirely and grind drills — speed matters more than understanding.

The mock on day one wastes your only baseline and demoralizes; random study leaves gaps the assessment will find. Drills without understanding produce fast wrong answers.
scenarios.hint: Think about what the scenarios assume you already know.

scenarios.title: When You Get Stuck
scenarios.situation: You have failed the same scenario three times. The explanation makes sense when you read it, but you keep choosing wrong under time pressure.
choices: Drop back to the lesson: re-read the concepts, write out the decision process in your own words, then re-attempt the scenario untimed before going timed again.
Keep re-attempting the scenario until you memorize the right answer.
Skip it and move on — one scenario will not decide the assessment.
Look up the answer online and move faster through the rest.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats repeated failure as a signal: the mental model is broken, not the memory. Rebuilding from the lesson concepts — in your own words — repairs the model. Memorizing the answer passes one scenario and fails the next variation. The assessment tests patterns, not instances.
scenarios.hint: Is the problem memory or the underlying mental model?
objectives: Repair mental models from lesson concepts
evidence: Scenario failed 3x: same wrong choice twice, different wrong choice once

scenarios.title: The Slow Training Loop
scenarios.situation: Your preprocessing script takes 40 minutes per run. Profiling shows 90% of time in a Python for-loop computing per-row features over 2 million rows.
choices: Vectorize with NumPy/pandas: rewrite the row loop as array operations so the work runs in compiled C code — typically a 50-100x speedup with no hardware change.
Buy a bigger machine — the loop is inherently slow.
Add multiprocessing around the loop.
Sample fewer rows to make it faster.
scenarios.why: The correct approach attacks the algorithmic bottleneck, not the hardware: Python-level loops over millions of rows are the classic ML slowdown, and vectorization removes the interpreter overhead entirely. Multiprocessing parallelizes the slowness; sampling changes the data. Vectorize first, then profile again.
scenarios.hint: Where does the 90% actually go — Python overhead or real computation?
evidence: 38 of 40 minutes in a single Python for-loop over DataFrame rows

scenarios.title: The Shape Error
scenarios.situation: Your distance code crashes: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (128,) and (128,1). You need pairwise distances between 128 vectors.
choices: Flatten both to 1D and subtract.
Reshape deliberately: x[:, None, :] - y[None, :, :] produces the (128,128,d) difference tensor, then reduce — understand each axis instead of guessing reshapes until it runs.
Loop over pairs in Python.
Use np.tile to manually expand both arrays.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats broadcasting as explicit axis algebra: adding new axes with None/unsqueeze makes the (128,128) pairwise structure intentional and readable. Flattening destroys the structure; tile wastes memory; the Python loop abandons the speedup you wanted.
scenarios.hint: What shape should the pairwise result be, and which axes produce it?
evidence: shapes (128,) and (128,1) not broadcastable in current expression

scenarios.title: The Warning That Lies
scenarios.situation: Your cleaning notebook runs but the filtered DataFrame is unchanged. Pandas emitted SettingWithCopyWarning, which you ignored.
scenarios.prompt: What happened and what is the fix?
choices: Pandas is buggy — restart the kernel and rerun.
The warning is cosmetic; the data is actually fine.
Chained assignment wrote to a temporary copy, not the original: df[df.x > 0]['y'] = 1 may silently do nothing. Fix with a single .loc call: df.loc[df.x > 0, 'y'] = 1.
Convert everything to NumPy arrays to avoid pandas quirks.
scenarios.why: The correct approach respects the warning as a real bug report: chained indexing returns a copy in unpredictable cases, so the assignment vanishes. A single .loc call is atomic and unambiguous. Ignoring warnings in data code is how models train on uncleaned data.
scenarios.hint: Did the assignment reach the original DataFrame or a copy?
evidence: df[df.x > 0]['y'] = 1 ran clean; df['y'] unchanged afterwards

scenarios.title: The Unrepeatable Win
scenarios.situation: Last Tuesday a training run hit 94.2% accuracy — your best ever. You reran the identical script and got 92.8%. Nothing in the code changed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
choices: The GPU is degrading — hardware fault.
94.2% was a measurement error; trust the lower number.
Someone edited the dataset between runs.
Unseeded randomness: data shuffling, weight initialization, or dropout sampled differently across runs. Seed random, NumPy, and the framework, and log the seed with the result.
scenarios.why: The correct approach names the usual suspect first: unseeded RNG state makes every run a different experiment, so 'best ever' is not a reproducible result. Full seeding plus logged seeds turns luck into science. Hardware faults and data edits are possible but far less likely than the randomness you never controlled.
scenarios.hint: What differs between two runs of identical code?
evidence: Same script, same data: 94.2% then 92.8%, no code change

scenarios.title: The 50 GB CSV
scenarios.situation: You need features from a 50 GB CSV on a 16 GB machine. pd.read_csv crashes with MemoryError every time.
choices: Stream it: pd.read_csv(..., chunksize=100_000) processes the file in bounded memory, aggregating per chunk — or use a generator pipeline so RAM stays flat regardless of file size.
Load it in 4 pieces and hope they fit.
Convert to Excel first — it compresses better.
Increase swap space to 64 GB and load it whole.
scenarios.why: The correct approach keeps memory bounded by design: chunked reading processes the file as a stream, so a 50 GB file needs only the chunk size in RAM. Swap-thrashing a full load is brutally slow; splitting by hand is fragile. Streaming is the general solution for data bigger than RAM.
scenarios.hint: Does any step truly need the whole file in memory at once?
evidence: 50 GB CSV, 16 GB RAM, need per-row features + global aggregates

scenarios.title: The Embedding Memory Bill
scenarios.situation: Your embedding table (2M vectors x 768 dims) uses 12 GB in float64. The serving machine has 8 GB total.
choices: Shard the table across 4 machines.
Downcast to float32: embeddings lose nothing measurable at 32-bit, halving memory to ~6 GB — and float16/bf16 halves it again if the serving stack supports it.
Reduce embedding dimension to 128 and retrain everything.
Compress with gzip — decompress per query.
scenarios.why: The correct approach questions the precision before the architecture: float64 for embeddings is almost never needed, and the downcast is free accuracy-wise. Sharding adds operational complexity for a problem a dtype change solves; retraining is weeks of work; per-query decompression destroys latency.
scenarios.hint: How much precision do cosine-similarity rankings actually need?
evidence: 2M x 768 x 8 bytes = 12.3 GB; x 4 bytes = 6.1 GB

scenarios.title: The Silent Corruption
scenarios.situation: Training loss decreases smoothly, but validation accuracy is stuck at chance. Shapes all check out. You suspect the data, not the model.
choices: Increase model capacity; chance-level means underfitting.
Train longer; validation will catch up.
Verify label alignment: confirm the labels actually correspond to the features — a shuffled or misjoined label column trains smoothly to exactly chance, with perfect-looking loss curves.
The validation set is too hard; make it easier.
scenarios.why: The correct approach suspects the silent bug: smooth training loss with chance-level validation and correct shapes is the signature of broken label alignment — the model learns the (wrong) mapping perfectly. Capacity and epochs cannot fix a correspondence problem; the check is joining a few rows back to source and eyeballing them.
scenarios.hint: If the model learned perfectly, what exactly did it learn?
evidence: Train loss smooth and low; val accuracy = chance; shapes correct

scenarios.title: The Too-Good Model
scenarios.situation: Your churn model scores 0.99 AUC in cross-validation. In production it performs at 0.62. Preprocessing was fit on the full dataset before the split.
choices: Target leakage through preprocessing: fitting the scaler/imputer on the full dataset let test-fold statistics influence training. Fit all preprocessing inside the pipeline so each fold learns only from its own training split.
Cross-validation is unreliable — use a single split instead.
The production data is just harder; 0.62 is the true score.
You need a more complex model to hold the 0.99.
scenarios.why: The correct approach identifies the classic leak: preprocessing fit on all data smuggles information across the train/test boundary, inflating validation scores that evaporate in production. sklearn Pipelines exist precisely to prevent this — transformers refit per fold on training data only. The 0.37 gap is the signature of leakage, not harder data.
scenarios.hint: What did the test folds 'know' that production data never will?
evidence: CV AUC 0.99 with pre-fit preprocessing; 0.62 in production

scenarios.title: Training-Serving Skew
scenarios.situation: Training used a notebook's cleaning functions; serving reimplemented them in the API. Predictions drift from offline evaluation on identical inputs.
choices: Add more logging to find the differing line.
Serialize the fitted pipeline as the deployable artifact: pickle the sklearn Pipeline (preprocessing + model) and load that exact object in the API — one implementation, used in both places.
Retrain the model on production data.
Write the cleaning code more carefully in the API.
scenarios.why: The correct approach eliminates the two-implementations problem at the root: the fitted pipeline object carries the exact fitted transformers, so serving cannot drift from training. Careful reimplementation still leaves two codebases to diverge; logging finds today's diff, not next month's.
scenarios.hint: How many implementations of the transform exist right now?
evidence: Same raw input -> different prediction offline vs API

scenarios.title: The Mystery Regression
scenarios.situation: After a routine retrain, accuracy dropped 4 points. Code is unchanged (same git hash). Nobody can say what data the new model trained on.
scenarios.prompt: What practice would have made this diagnosable in minutes?
choices: Retrain again and hope it recovers.
Blame the random seed and rerun with more seeds.
Dataset hashing and manifests: log the dataset SHA-256, row count, and generation query with every run, so you can diff the old and new training data immediately.
Add more features to recover the accuracy.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats training data as a versioned input: with hashes logged, the diagnosis is a manifest diff (new source added? date range shifted? rows dropped?) instead of an archaeology project. Same code plus unknown data equals an unanswerable question — the hash makes the data known.
scenarios.hint: What are the two inputs to training, and which one can you currently name?
evidence: Code hash identical; training data described as 'the usual folder'

scenarios.title: The Stale Model
scenarios.situation: The fraud model was last retrained 5 months ago. Fraud patterns shifted; losses are climbing. Retraining is a manual notebook run 'when someone has time.'
choices: Retrain manually right now and set a calendar reminder.
Hire someone whose job is retraining models.
Freeze the model — retraining risks making it worse.
Orchestrate it: a scheduled DAG that ingests, validates, retrains, evaluates against a promotion gate, and alerts on failure — retraining becomes automatic with human oversight only on exceptions.
scenarios.why: The correct approach removes human memory from the loop: a scheduled pipeline with validation gates retrains reliably, and the promotion gate (new model must beat current on holdout) makes automation safe. Calendar reminders rot; freezing the model surrenders to drift.
scenarios.hint: What happens the next time everyone is busy?
evidence: Last retrain 5 months ago; fraud loss +18% since

scenarios.title: The Divergent Feature
scenarios.situation: The 'days_since_last_login' feature is computed in SQL for training and in Python for serving. Off-by-one differences are corrupting predictions.
scenarios.prompt: What architectural pattern fixes this class of bug permanently?
choices: Single-source feature logic: compute the feature once in a shared function or feature store, and have both training and serving call it — one definition, zero divergence.
Write better SQL to match the Python exactly.
Add a test comparing SQL and Python outputs nightly.
Drop the feature — it is not worth the trouble.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes dual implementation as the disease: two definitions of one feature will diverge, and nightly diff tests only detect divergence after damage. A single shared computation (function or feature store) makes divergence structurally impossible.
scenarios.hint: Why will the SQL and Python eventually disagree again?
objectives: Use a single source of truth
evidence: SQL: DATEDIFF(day,...) vs Python: (d2-d1).days — off-by-one on same-day logins

scenarios.title: The Silent Failure
scenarios.situation: The weekly retrain DAG failed at the ingest stage three weeks ago. Nobody noticed; the model kept serving stale predictions.
choices: More frequent retraining would have masked it.

Failure alerting on the pipeline: every stage needs success/failure visibility, retries for transient errors, and a page when a stage fails terminally — a pipeline nobody watches is a pipeline that fails silently.
The model should have kept working — alerting is overhead.
Manual checks of the model each Monday.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats observability as part of the pipeline: scheduled work without alerting is scheduled failure. Retries handle the transient; alerts handle the terminal; a dashboard shows stage health at a glance. Manual Monday checks are the pre-automation habit that automation was supposed to replace.
scenarios.hint: How long can a stage fail before anyone knows?
evidence: Ingest failed 3 weeks ago; discovered during a quarterly review

scenarios.title: The Schema Change
scenarios.situation: Upstream renamed 'user_age' to 'age_years' overnight. The pipeline ran, the model trained on a column of NaNs (missing column -> all-null after merge), and nobody noticed for a week.
scenarios.prompt: What test would have caught this on the first run?
choices: More training data would have absorbed the missing column.
The model should be robust to missing columns.
An ingest data contract asserting the exact expected column set: set(df.columns) == EXPECTED_COLS fails immediately on the rename, failing the run loudly instead of training on NaNs.
A bigger validation set would have caught it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach puts the contract at the boundary: schema assertions at ingest turn silent corruption into a loud, immediate failure naming the stage. Robustness to missing columns is a separate feature; validation sets evaluate models, not pipelines; more data just means more NaN-trained rows.
scenarios.hint: Where should the pipeline have complained — and did it?
evidence: Column renamed upstream; pipeline trained on NaNs for a week silently

scenarios.title: The 99% Mirage
scenarios.situation: Your classifier hits 99% training accuracy but 71% validation. More epochs keep widening the gap.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnosis and the fix?
choices: Classic overfitting: the model memorizes training noise. Stop training on validation plateau (early stopping), add regularization, or get more training data — more epochs only deepen the memorization.
Underfitting — train longer with a bigger model.
The validation set is corrupted; rebuild it.
99% training accuracy proves the model is good; ship it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach reads the gap, not the headline number: a 28-point train/validation split with a widening trend is overfitting by definition. Early stopping halts at the validation optimum; regularization constrains memorization. Training longer feeds the disease, and shipping a memorizing model ships 71% production accuracy.
scenarios.hint: What does the widening gap tell you that 99% does not?
evidence: Train 99%, validation 71%, gap widening with epochs

scenarios.title: Testing on Training Data
scenarios.situation: A teammate reports 97% accuracy, evaluated on the same data the model trained on. They want to ship.
choices: Nothing — 97% is excellent, ship it.
The evaluation is meaningless: accuracy on training data measures memorization capacity, not generalization. Re-evaluate on a held-out test set the model has never seen before deciding anything.
The model is underfit; 97% is too low for training data.
Use cross-validation on the training data instead.
scenarios.why: The correct approach insists on the basic contract: performance claims require unseen data. Training accuracy can hit 100% with a lookup table that fails on everything new. The held-out test set is the only honest estimate — everything else is optimism.
scenarios.hint: What would a pure memorization table score on this evaluation?

scenarios.title: The Exploding Loss
scenarios.situation: Two epochs in, your loss jumps from 2.3 to NaN. The learning rate is 0.1 with a deep network.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: The data contains NaNs — clean it first.
The model needs more epochs to settle.
Learning rate too high: the optimizer steps past the minimum into divergence, and gradients overflow to NaN. Drop the learning rate by 10-100x (try 1e-3) and watch the curve stabilize.
Switch to a different framework.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches symptom to cause: loss exploding to NaN within epochs of starting, at lr=0.1 on a deep net, is the textbook too-large-step divergence. Data NaNs usually show up as NaN from step one or not at all; more epochs cannot fix a diverging trajectory.
scenarios.hint: What changed between the healthy loss at 2.3 and the NaN?

scenarios.title: Shuffling Time
scenarios.situation: You shuffled a 3-year transaction history randomly into train/val/test. Validation accuracy is stellar. Live performance is poor.
choices: Three years of data is insufficient; collect more.
The live data distribution changed; nothing was wrong with the split.
Shuffling is standard practice; the issue is elsewhere.

Temporal leakage: random shuffling lets the model train on future transactions and 'predict' past ones — information flows backward in time. Split chronologically: train on the earliest period, validate and test on later ones.
scenarios.why: The correct approach respects causality: in production the model only ever sees the past when predicting the future, so evaluation must replicate that. Random splits on time-ordered data hand the model future knowledge — the stellar validation score measured time travel, not skill. Chronological splits are non-negotiable for temporal data.
scenarios.hint: In production, will the model ever see the future at prediction time?
evidence: Random 80/10/10 split on 2023-2026 transactions; live = 2026-10 onward

scenarios.title: The 95% Trap
scenarios.situation: Fraud is 5% of transactions. Your model predicts 'not fraud' always and scores 95% accuracy. The team celebrates.
choices: Accuracy lies on imbalanced data: a constant 'not fraud' classifier scores 95% while catching zero fraud. Evaluate with precision, recall, and F1 — and consider class weights or resampling so the model actually learns the minority class.
95% accuracy is genuinely good; the model works.
The model needs more features to beat 95%.
Fraud is too rare to model; use rules instead.
scenarios.why: The correct approach exposes the degenerate solution: always predicting the majority class is the laziest possible model, and accuracy rewards it. Recall on the fraud class is the business metric — it is currently zero. Precision/recall, PR curves, and class-weighted training turn the optimization toward actually detecting fraud.
scenarios.hint: What is the model's recall on the fraud class?
evidence: Fraud class: 0 predicted correctly out of 5,000 actual

scenarios.title: Tuning Against Test
scenarios.situation: After 200 hyperparameter trials evaluated on the test set, test accuracy rose from 88% to 91%. The final report cites 91%.
choices: Nothing — 91% beats 88%, the tuning worked.
The test set became a validation set: 200 rounds of selection against it overfit the hyperparameters to its quirks. The 91% is optimistic; you need a fresh held-out set for an honest final number.
200 trials is too few; run 2,000 for a better number.
The report should cite 88% as the baseline instead.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes test-set overfitting: each trial is a tiny peek, and 200 peeks accumulate into fitting the test set's noise. The reported 91% will not reproduce on truly new data. Tune against validation, lock test away, and evaluate once — or collect a fresh holdout for the final estimate.
scenarios.hint: How many times did the tuning process 'see' the test set?
evidence: 200 trials, model selected by test accuracy each round

scenarios.title: The Small Dataset
scenarios.situation: You have 800 labeled images for a defect-detection task. Training from scratch plateaus at 72% accuracy.
choices: Collect 50,000 more labeled images.
Use a bigger architecture trained from scratch.

Transfer learning: start from a pretrained vision backbone, train a new head on your 800 images (frozen backbone first, then gentle unfreezing) — 800 images is plenty for fine-tuning, starvation rations for from-scratch.
72% is the ceiling for this task; ship it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches the method to the data regime: 800 images cannot train a deep network from scratch, but they can absolutely fine-tune a pretrained backbone whose early layers already understand vision. Data collection at 60x is months of work; bigger from-scratch architectures starve identically.
scenarios.hint: What do the early layers of a pretrained model already know?

domains.name: Inference & Serving

scenarios.title: Fraud at Checkout
scenarios.situation: A payment fraud model must approve or block transactions while the customer waits. The team proposes a nightly batch job scoring the day's transactions.
choices: The decision latency demands online inference: fraud must be scored in milliseconds during checkout — a nightly batch scores transactions hours after the money moved. Build an online API with a sub-100ms budget.
Batch is fine — fraud can be reviewed the next day.
The model needs retraining, not re-serving.
Nightly batch is cheaper, so it is the right call.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches serving mode to decision latency: the fraud decision happens at checkout, so the prediction must too. Batch is cheaper per prediction but useless after the fact — the cost metric that matters is fraud prevented, not predictions per dollar. Online API with warm replicas and a latency SLO is the only mode that intercepts the transaction.
scenarios.hint: When is the decision made — before or after the batch runs?
objectives: Match serving mode to decision latency

scenarios.title: The Per-Request Load
scenarios.situation: The prediction API takes 2.5 seconds per request under load but 40ms in testing. Code review shows load_model() called inside the request handler.
choices: Add more replicas to spread the 2.5s load.

Load once at startup: move model loading out of the handler into app initialization so requests share one loaded model — the 2.5s was disk + deserialization per request plus memory churn under concurrency.
Cache predictions to avoid loading.
Buy faster disks for model loading.
scenarios.why: The correct approach removes the per-request tax at its source: model loading belongs in startup, period. More replicas multiply the waste; caching dodges it for repeated inputs only; faster disks shave the symptom. The 40ms test number was the truth — production just never got to see it because every request reloaded.
scenarios.hint: What work repeats identically on every single request?
evidence: 2.46s of 2.5s per request inside load_model(); test path: 40ms

scenarios.title: The Crash at 3 AM
scenarios.situation: The API crashed overnight. Logs show a client sent a feature as a string instead of a number; the preprocessing threw and the worker died, dropping all in-flight requests.
choices: Blame the client for sending bad data.
Wrap everything in try/except and return 200 anyway.
Boundary validation: a schema check on every request that rejects malformed input with a 400 before it reaches the model — one bad client must never kill the worker serving everyone else.
Restart workers on a cron every hour.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats the API boundary as a trust boundary: validate types, ranges, and required fields up front, reject with 400 and a clear message. try/except-everything hides real bugs; hourly restarts institutionalize the crash; blaming the client does not keep the service up. Validation is the bulkhead between one bad request and all good ones.
scenarios.hint: Whose fault is the crash — the client's data or the missing validation?
evidence: ValueError in preprocessing: could not convert string to float; worker exited

scenarios.title: Optimizing Blind
scenarios.situation: p99 latency is 900ms against a 250ms budget. The team wants to rewrite the API in a faster language.
choices: Rewrite in the faster language — it is clearly too slow.
Add GPUs; inference must be the bottleneck.
Increase the budget to 900ms.
Measure the slices: instrument network, deserialization, preprocessing, inference, and serialization separately — then optimize the biggest slice. A rewrite gambles months on an unmeasured hunch.
scenarios.why: The correct approach refuses to optimize blind: if inference is 700ms of the 900, quantization or batching fixes it; if preprocessing is 600ms, the language rewrite was aimed at the wrong slice entirely. Measurement first is not caution — it is the difference between a fix and an expensive guess.
scenarios.hint: Which slice is actually slow — do you know, or are you guessing?
evidence: p99 900ms vs 250ms budget; no per-stage timings exist

scenarios.title: The Launch Spike
scenarios.situation: Marketing launches tomorrow; traffic will spike 10x for 6 hours. The API runs 2 fixed replicas sized for normal traffic.
choices: Pre-scale plus autoscaling: raise to 8 replicas before launch, enable autoscaling on p99 latency with a floor of 4, and load-test the 10x ramp today — discover the breaking point before users do.
Hope the 2 replicas hold; scale if they fall over.
Turn off the marketing launch.
Add replicas manually when alerts fire.
scenarios.why: The correct approach prepares for known spikes instead of reacting to them: pre-scaling covers the immediate surge, autoscaling handles variance, and today's load test finds the real ceiling. Reactive scaling during a spike means the first wave of users experiences the outage that triggers the scale-up.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the first 10,000 users while you manually add replicas?
evidence: 10x traffic for 6h starting 09:00 tomorrow; current: 2 fixed replicas

scenarios.title: The Risky Upgrade
scenarios.situation: Model v5 beats v4 offline by 2 points. The team wants to swap it into production Friday afternoon.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe deployment path?
choices: Swap it Friday — offline gains are proven gains.

Shadow then canary: run v5 on live traffic without serving its answers to validate real-world behavior, then route 5% of traffic, compare live metrics, and roll forward — or back in seconds via routing.
Wait until Monday, then swap 100%.
A/B test by asking users which predictions they prefer.
scenarios.why: The correct approach earns production trust gradually: shadow mode reveals real-world surprises (data quirks offline eval never saw) with zero user impact, and the canary limits blast radius while live metrics confirm the gain. Friday full swaps convert a 2-point offline win into a potential all-weekend incident.
scenarios.hint: What could differ between offline eval and live traffic?
evidence: 100% traffic swap to v5, Friday 16:00, no rollback plan

scenarios.title: Which Model Said That?
scenarios.situation: A customer disputes a decision from last month. You cannot determine which model version produced it.
choices: Keep only the latest model; old versions do not matter.
Ask the customer to reproduce the request.
Log and return the model version with every prediction: the response carries model_version, and the prediction log stores input hash, version, output, and timestamp — every decision is attributable.
Version models by date in the filename.
scenarios.why: The correct approach makes predictions attributable by construction: version in the response plus a prediction log means any historical decision maps to its exact model and inputs in one lookup. Filename dating is not queryable; asking the customer to reproduce is not serious; keeping only the latest destroys the evidence.
scenarios.hint: How would you answer the dispute with only today's model available?
evidence: Decision from 2026-09-12; 3 model versions shipped since

domains.name: Vector Databases & Embeddings

scenarios.title: Most Similar Pair
scenarios.situation: You have three normalized embedding vectors: A=[1,0], B=[0.8,0.6], C=[0,1]. A query matches A exactly.
scenarios.prompt: Which is most similar to the query, by cosine similarity?
choices: B: cosine(A,B) = 0.8, versus cosine(A,C) = 0 — B is far more similar. The query matching A exactly means similarity to A is 1.0, and B's 0.8 beats C's 0.
C, because it is also a unit vector.
A and C are equally similar since both are axis-aligned.
B and C tie at 0.5.
scenarios.why: The correct approach computes: cosine similarity of unit vectors is their dot product. A·B = 0.8, A·C = 0. B is clearly most similar. 'Both are unit vectors' is irrelevant — cosine already normalizes; direction is what matters, and B points mostly along A while C is orthogonal.
scenarios.hint: For unit vectors, cosine similarity is just the dot product. Compute both.

scenarios.title: The Missing Answer
scenarios.situation: Your RAG system cannot answer questions whose answers sit near page boundaries. Chunks are 1000 characters with zero overlap.
choices: Increase chunk size to 5000 characters.

Add overlap (10-20%) and prefer structural chunking: boundary answers get split across chunks with zero overlap, so no single chunk contains the full answer. Overlap guarantees boundary content appears whole somewhere.
Increase top-k from 5 to 50.
Use a bigger embedding model.
scenarios.why: The correct approach diagnoses the mechanism: with zero overlap, any answer spanning a chunk boundary is fragmented across two chunks, and neither chunk alone supports the answer. Overlap is the direct fix; structural chunking (split on paragraphs) avoids mid-idea cuts entirely. Bigger chunks dilute precision; bigger k adds noise; the embedding model was never the problem.
scenarios.hint: Where exactly do the failing answers live in the documents?
evidence: All failures: answer text spans a 1000-char chunk boundary

scenarios.title: 10 Million Vectors
scenarios.situation: Exact search over 10M vectors takes 4 seconds per query. The SLA is 200ms. Recall must stay above 95%.
choices: Buy a bigger machine for exact search.
Reduce to 1M vectors by sampling.
Build an ANN index (HNSW): approximate nearest neighbor search returns in milliseconds at 95%+ recall@k — the standard solution at this scale, tuned until recall meets the bar.
Cache all queries.
scenarios.why: The correct approach accepts the exact/approximate tradeoff: exact O(n) scan cannot hit 200ms at 10M vectors on any reasonable hardware, while HNSW traverses a graph instead of scanning, hitting milliseconds with tunable recall. Measure recall@k after building — the 95% bar is verifiable, not hoped for.
scenarios.hint: What does exact search cost per query, fundamentally?
evidence: 10M vectors x 768 dims; exact: 4s/query; SLA: 200ms, recall >= 95%

scenarios.title: The Model Swap
scenarios.situation: The team upgraded the embedding model. Search quality collapsed overnight — relevant documents no longer surface.
choices: The new model is worse; roll back immediately.
The index needs more RAM for the new model.
Queries need to be longer for the new model.

Embedding space incompatibility: the index holds vectors from the old model, but queries now embed with the new one — the coordinates live in different spaces, so similarity is meaningless. Re-embed the entire corpus with the new model and rebuild the index.
scenarios.why: The correct approach names the mechanism: embedding models define their own coordinate spaces, and cross-model comparison is geometric nonsense. The fix is a full re-embedding pipeline — corpus through the new model, index rebuilt — ideally versioned alongside the model so this never happens silently again.
scenarios.hint: Which model produced the vectors sitting in the index right now?
evidence: Model swapped Tuesday; index built last month; queries embed with new model

scenarios.title: Grounded Hallucination
scenarios.situation: RAG retrieves the correct chunks, but the generator still invents facts not present in them.
scenarios.prompt: Where is the failure and what is the fix?
choices: Generation ignoring context: retrieval worked, so the fix is in the generation stage — strengthen the 'answer ONLY from context' instruction, lower temperature, and require citations; evaluate citation fidelity separately from retrieval quality.
Retrieve more chunks (k=20).
The embedding model is bad; replace it.
Chunk size is wrong; re-chunk everything.
scenarios.why: The correct approach localizes the failure using the pipeline's three stages: correct chunks + wrong answer = generation problem. More chunks add noise to a generator already ignoring context; the embedding model did its job. Constrain the generator (explicit grounding instruction, citations, lower temperature) and measure whether answers stay inside the provided text.
scenarios.hint: If retrieval is correct, which stage remains suspect?
evidence: Correct chunks retrieved (verified); answer contains facts absent from all chunks

scenarios.title: The Leak
scenarios.situation: An employee asked about layoffs and the RAG system quoted an internal HR memo they were not cleared to see.
choices: The HR memo should not have been indexed at all.
Access control in retrieval: authorization filters must apply before ranking — never retrieve, rank, or show chunks the user cannot access, regardless of similarity score.
The user should not have asked about layoffs.
The LLM should have refused to answer.
scenarios.why: The correct approach puts authorization in the retrieval path as a hard filter: similarity must never override access control. Not indexing the memo destroys legitimate HR use; relying on the LLM to refuse is a hope, not a control. Filter-then-rank with the user's permissions is the structural fix.
scenarios.hint: At what point could the memo have been excluded — and was it?
evidence: Restricted HR memo quoted to unauthorized employee via RAG answer

scenarios.title: The Part Number Problem
scenarios.situation: Users search for exact part numbers like 'XJ-4471'. Pure vector search returns 'XJ-4472' and 'XJ-4470' as 'similar' — wrong parts, confidently.
choices: Train a custom embedding model on part numbers.
Tell users to search descriptions instead of part numbers.

Hybrid retrieval: fuse dense vector search (meaning) with BM25 keyword search (exact terms) — the keyword side nails exact part numbers while vectors handle semantic queries. Reciprocal rank fusion merges both lists.
Increase embedding dimensions to 1536.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes the modality mismatch: embeddings are built for semantic similarity, which is exactly wrong for exact identifiers where 'similar' means 'incorrect'. BM25 treats 'XJ-4471' as the literal token it is. Hybrid gives both behaviors; custom training is months of work for what keyword search does today.
scenarios.hint: Is a part number a meaning or a token?
evidence: Exact-code queries return near-miss codes with high similarity scores

domains.name: GPU Compute

scenarios.title: CUDA Out of Memory
scenarios.situation: Training crashes at epoch 3 with CUDA out of memory. Batch size is 128 on a 24GB GPU. The model itself is 4GB in fp16.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most practical first response?
choices: Halve the batch size and add gradient accumulation: batch 64 with 2 accumulation steps keeps the effective batch at 128 while roughly halving activation memory — no model or hardware change needed.
Buy a bigger GPU immediately.
Switch to a smaller model.
Reduce the learning rate.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats batch size as the VRAM dial it is: activations scale with batch, so halving it frees large memory, and gradient accumulation preserves the effective batch size the optimizer sees. New hardware is weeks away; a smaller model changes the experiment; learning rate does not affect memory at all.
scenarios.hint: What grows with batch size — weights, or activations?
evidence: CUDA OOM at epoch 3; model 4GB fp16; batch 128; GPU 24GB

scenarios.title: The Idle GPU
scenarios.situation: nvidia-smi shows 22% GPU utilization during training. The run takes 3x longer than estimated. CPU is pegged at 100%.
choices: The GPU is too slow; upgrade it.
Data loading bottleneck: the GPU starves while a single process decodes data on CPU. Add loader workers, enable pinned memory and prefetching — the fix is in the input pipeline, not the model.
The model is too small to utilize the GPU.
Increase batch size to fill the GPU.
scenarios.why: The correct approach reads the two metrics together: low GPU util plus pegged CPU is the signature of a starved accelerator. Loader workers parallelize the CPU-bound decoding so the GPU never waits. A bigger GPU idles identically; batch size cannot fix a feed problem.
scenarios.hint: If the GPU is waiting, what is it waiting for?

scenarios.title: Sizing the Job
scenarios.situation: You need to train a 3B-parameter model in fp16 with Adam. Available: 24GB GPUs and 80GB GPUs.
scenarios.prompt: Which do you need, and why?
choices: 24GB is fine — 3B parameters is small.
24GB with a tiny batch size will fit.
80GB: weights 6GB + gradients 6GB + Adam states 24GB ≈ 36GB before activations — it cannot fit on 24GB. The 4x rule (params x bytes x 4) decides before you rent anything.
It depends only on the dataset size.
scenarios.why: The correct approach does the arithmetic: 3B params x 2 bytes = 6GB weights, another 6GB gradients, Adam keeps two fp32 states per param = 24GB — 36GB total before activations, which grow with batch and sequence length. No batch size shrinks the optimizer states. Estimate first, provision second.
scenarios.hint: What must fit in VRAM besides the weights?

scenarios.title: The Silent Stall
scenarios.situation: After enabling fp16 mixed precision, loss decreases normally for 50 steps, then flatlines. Gradients inspected: nearly all zeros.
choices: The model converged in 50 steps.
Learning rate is too high.
The data ran out.
Gradient underflow: fp16's tiny representable range rounds small gradients to zero. Enable loss scaling (or switch to bf16) so gradients survive in representable range.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes fp16's range limits: gradients smaller than ~6e-8 become zero, so learning silently stops while loss looks 'stable'. Loss scaling multiplies the loss before backprop, lifting gradients into representable range, then unscales before the update. bf16 avoids the issue with fp32-like exponent range.
scenarios.hint: What is the smallest positive value fp16 can represent?
evidence: fp16 enabled; gradients ~0 after step 50; loss flatlined, not converged

scenarios.title: GPU for a Tiny Model
scenarios.situation: A logistic regression on 10k rows runs slower on GPU than CPU. The team wants a bigger GPU.
choices: Stay on CPU: transfer overhead dominates tiny workloads — moving data to the GPU costs more than the computation saves. Bigger GPUs make the ratio worse, not better.
Get the bigger GPU; GPUs are always faster.
Increase the data to 10M rows to justify the GPU.
The GPU drivers are misconfigured.
scenarios.why: The correct approach benchmarks instead of assuming: for small models and batches, PCIe transfer time exceeds compute time, so the GPU can never win. The fix is matching hardware to workload — CPU for the tiny job, GPU where the math dominates. Padding the dataset to justify hardware is backwards.
scenarios.hint: Where does wall-clock time actually go at this scale?

scenarios.title: Four GPUs, 1.5x Speedup
scenarios.situation: Data-parallel training on 4 GPUs yields only 1.5x speedup over 1 GPU. Interconnect is standard Ethernet.
choices: The GPUs are defective.

Gradient synchronization over slow networking: all-reduce across 4 GPUs on Ethernet spends more time communicating than the extra compute saves. Faster interconnect (or fewer, bigger batches per step) restores scaling.
Data parallel is the wrong strategy; use model parallel.
The dataset is too small.
scenarios.why: The correct approach identifies communication as the tax: every step all-reduces full gradients across all GPUs, and Ethernet bandwidth turns that into the dominant cost. The compute scaled 4x; the communication did not. Interconnect is the first thing to check when multi-GPU scaling disappoints.
scenarios.hint: What happens between the backward pass and the optimizer step?

scenarios.title: The Learning Rate After Scaling
scenarios.situation: You went from 1 GPU (batch 32) to 4 GPUs (effective batch 128) with data parallel. Training is now unstable — loss oscillates wildly.
choices: Four GPUs are inherently unstable; go back to one.
The data shards differ; reshuffle.
Learning rate not scaled with batch size: 4x the batch with the same LR overshoots. Scale LR roughly linearly with batch size (with warmup) and re-stabilize.
Gradient averaging is buggy; sum instead.
scenarios.why: The correct approach applies the linear scaling rule: effective batch quadrupled, so each step averages 4x the data and the old step size overshoots — hence oscillation. Scale the learning rate up proportionally (often with a short warmup) to match the new batch dynamics. The hardware is fine; the hyperparameters did not follow the batch size.
scenarios.hint: What changed about each optimizer step when the batch quadrupled?
evidence: 1x32 -> 4x32 data parallel; LR unchanged; loss oscillating

domains.name: Experiment Tracking

scenarios.title: The Unrepeatable Best
scenarios.situation: Your best run (F1 0.91) cannot be reproduced. The log has the metric and hyperparameters but no code version, dataset hash, or seeds.
choices: Provenance: without the git hash, dataset hash, environment pins, and seeds, the result is unmoored — you cannot know what code, data, or randomness produced it. Log all four with every run going forward.
A better model — 0.91 was probably luck anyway.
More compute to rerun the search.
The metric was miscalculated; ignore it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats the 0.91 as lost and fixes the system: reproducibility needs code + data + environment + seeds, and this log has none of them. The metric without provenance is trivia — it cannot be rebuilt, defended, or shipped. Every future run logs the full quartet.
scenarios.hint: What would you need to replay that exact run?

scenarios.title: The Unfair Comparison
scenarios.situation: Run A (F1 0.85) used validation split v1; Run B (F1 0.87) used split v2 and a different learning rate. The team ships B.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this decision?
choices: Nothing — 0.87 beats 0.85.
Confounded comparison: B differs in split AND learning rate, so the +0.02 could come from an easier split, not a better model. Compare on identical data with one variable changed.
B should have used an even higher learning rate.
A's split was probably harder; B is fine.
scenarios.why: The correct approach demands controlled comparisons: two variables changed, zero attribution possible. The +0.02 might be pure split luck. Rerun B's config on split v1 (or both on a fixed split) before any ship decision — otherwise you are shipping noise.
scenarios.hint: How many variables differ between A and B?
evidence: A: split v1, lr 1e-3 -> 0.85; B: split v2, lr 3e-3 -> 0.87

scenarios.title: The Overwritten Champion
scenarios.situation: The production model file model.pkl was overwritten by a new training run. The new model performs worse, and the old weights are gone.
scenarios.prompt: What practice prevents this class of incident?
choices: Keep backups of model.pkl on a USB drive.
Name files with dates: model-2026-10-10.pkl.

Immutable versioned artifacts in a registry: every trained model gets a unique version (never overwritten), with lineage and stage labels — rollback is selecting the previous version, not mourning it.
Do not retrain production models.
scenarios.why: The correct approach makes overwriting structurally impossible: the registry assigns immutable versions, so 'the new run' creates v5 while v4 stays intact and staged. Date-stamped filenames help but lack lineage and gates; USB backups are not a system. Version immutability turns this incident into a non-event.
scenarios.hint: What does rollback require that no longer exists?
evidence: model.pkl overwritten; previous weights unrecoverable; rollback impossible

scenarios.title: The Lucky Best
scenarios.situation: After 60 random configs, the best validation F1 is 0.89 (+0.04 over baseline). The team reports 0.89 as the expected production performance.
choices: 60 configs is too few; the true best is higher.
Random search is unreliable; use grid search.
0.89 is fine — more trials means better estimates.

Multiple-comparisons bias: the max of 60 noisy evaluations overestimates the true mean — some config was bound to get lucky. Report the estimate from a fresh holdout set, or average the top few across seeds.
scenarios.why: The correct approach corrects for selection: taking the maximum over many noisy measurements biases upward — this is statistics, not pessimism. A fresh holdout (untouched during the search) gives the honest number. Celebrating the max is how teams ship 0.89 and observe 0.85.
scenarios.hint: If you rolled 60 dice and reported the highest, would you expect to roll it again?
evidence: 60 configs, best val F1 0.89; reported as expected performance

scenarios.title: The Data Changed Underneath
scenarios.situation: Two runs with identical code and params score 0.84 and 0.79. The dataset folder was 'updated' between them by a teammate.
scenarios.prompt: What would have made this a 5-minute diagnosis?
choices: Dataset hashes in the run log: diffing the two runs' data_sha values immediately shows the data changed — then diff the manifests (row counts, date ranges) to find what. Without hashes, you debug code for a data problem.
Lock the dataset folder so nobody can update it.
Rerun both until they agree.
Average the two scores and move on.
scenarios.why: The correct approach makes data changes visible: the hash diff proves the cause in seconds, and the manifest diff (rows added? dates shifted?) names it. Identical code plus different data is supposed to give different results — the bug was invisibility, not the update. Hash every dataset, log it every run.
scenarios.hint: The code is identical — so what input differs?
evidence: Same code+params: 0.84 then 0.79; 'data folder updated' between

scenarios.title: The Unproven Promotion
scenarios.situation: A new model beats the champion by 0.002 F1 on holdout. An engineer wants to promote it to production tonight.
scenarios.prompt: What should the promotion gate say?
choices: Promote — any improvement is an improvement.
Reject: +0.002 is within noise — the gate requires beating the champion by a meaningful margin plus passing latency and fairness checks. Promoting noise churns production for zero expected gain.
Promote, but only for 10% of traffic.
Tune it a bit more first, then promote.
scenarios.why: The correct approach enforces the margin: gates exist precisely to stop noise-driven churn. A 0.002 delta on a finite holdout is indistinguishable from luck, and each promotion carries regression risk. The gate's margin (e.g., +0.005) plus SLO checks turns promotion from opinion into policy.
scenarios.hint: Is +0.002 signal or noise on this holdout size?
evidence: Requires +0.005 holdout margin + p99 < 200ms + fairness pass

scenarios.title: The Repeated Dead End
scenarios.situation: Three engineers independently tried and abandoned the same feature idea over two months. Each spent a week.
scenarios.prompt: What process failure caused this waste?
choices: The engineers should communicate more in standup.
The idea was worth retrying — maybe it works now.

No shared experiment history: without a team-visible log of hypotheses, runs, and decisions, dead ends get rediscovered. A shared log with decision entries turns one person's week into everyone's lesson.
Feature ideas should be approved by a manager first.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats the shared log as team memory: 'tried 2026-08, failed because X' in a visible decision log stops the second and third attempts cold. Standups do not preserve knowledge across months; approval gates add bureaucracy without memory. Write it down where the team looks.
scenarios.hint: Where would the second engineer have seen the first attempt?
evidence: Same abandoned idea attempted 3x, ~3 engineer-weeks total

domains.name: Data Preparation

scenarios.title: The Skewed Imputation
scenarios.situation: Income column: median $52k, mean $91k (a few huge outliers). 8% missing. A teammate imputes with the mean.
choices: Mean imputation on skewed data injects outlier-distorted values: $91k is not a typical income, so missing rows get unrepresentative values. Median ($52k) is robust — use it, or better, model-based imputation.
Nothing — mean is the standard imputation.
8% missing is too much; drop the column.
Impute with $0; missing means no income.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches the imputation to the distribution: with heavy right skew, the mean describes the outliers, not the typical row. Median imputation keeps the filled values representative. The deeper fix is asking why income is missing (MNAR would need modeling), but median beats mean regardless.
scenarios.hint: Which statistic describes a typical row here — $52k or $91k?

scenarios.title: The Inflated Score
scenarios.situation: Validation F1 is 0.94. You discover 12% of rows are exact duplicates, and deduping happened AFTER the train/test split.
choices: 0.94 is still valid — duplicates are real data.

Leakage via duplicates: identical rows sit in both train and test, so the model is partly evaluated on memorized rows — 0.94 is inflated. Dedupe before splitting, then re-evaluate for the honest number.
Remove duplicates only from the test set.
The model is just good; duplicates do not matter.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes the mechanism: a duplicated row in train lets the model memorize it, and its twin in test rewards the memorization. The honest protocol is dedupe-first, split-second. Expect the re-evaluated score to drop — that drop was always the truth.
scenarios.hint: What does the model score on a test row identical to a training row?
evidence: 12% exact duplicates; dedupe ran after split; val F1 0.94

scenarios.title: The Color Order
scenarios.situation: A teammate ordinal-encodes car colors: red=0, blue=1, green=2, black=3. The model now treats black as 'more than' red.
choices: The order is wrong — black should be 0.
Colors should be dropped; they carry no signal.

False ordinality: colors have no natural order, but integer encoding invents one — the model learns spurious magnitude relationships. Use one-hot encoding for nominal categories; reserve ordinal for genuinely ordered values.
Use larger integers for better separation.
scenarios.why: The correct approach distinguishes nominal from ordinal: sizes (S<M<L) have real order; colors do not. Integer-encoded colors inject a lie the model will happily exploit. One-hot gives each color its own independent column with no invented ranking.
scenarios.hint: Is red 'less than' blue in any meaningful sense?

scenarios.title: The Helpful Teammate
scenarios.situation: A teammate 'helpfully' fit the StandardScaler on the full dataset before you split it, 'so all the data is normalized consistently.'
choices: It is fine — scaling is just preprocessing, not learning.
Only redo it if the test set is large.
Fit it on the test set instead for consistency.

Test statistics leaked into training: the scaler's mean and variance now encode information from the test set, so the training representation was shaped by data the model should never have seen. Refit on train only.
scenarios.why: The correct approach is uncompromising about the boundary: any statistic computed from test data and applied to training is leakage, however 'harmless' it feels. The scaler must learn its parameters from training data alone. 'Consistent normalization' is achieved by applying the frozen train scaler everywhere.
scenarios.hint: Whose mean and variance is the scaler using?

scenarios.title: The Too-Good Feature
scenarios.situation: Feature 'support_tickets_after_signup' has 0.97 feature importance for predicting 30-day churn. Everything else is under 0.05.
choices: Target leakage: tickets filed AFTER signup within the 30-day outcome window contain post-outcome information — at prediction time (day 0) these tickets do not exist yet. Rebuild the feature from pre-prediction data only.
A great feature — double down on ticket data.
The importance calculation is buggy.
Churn is just easy to predict.
scenarios.why: The correct approach applies the temporal test: could you compute this feature at the moment of prediction? Day-0 prediction cannot see day-15 tickets. The 0.97 importance is the model exploiting time travel, and production (no future tickets available) will collapse. Features must be computable from information available at prediction time.
scenarios.hint: At prediction time, do these tickets exist yet?

scenarios.title: Scaling for Trees
scenarios.situation: The team scales all features with StandardScaler before training a gradient-boosted tree model, adding a full preprocessing stage.
choices: Keep it — scaling never hurts.

Skip it: tree splits are threshold-based and scale-invariant — scaling changes nothing about the splits, so the stage adds complexity with zero benefit. Save scaling for distance/gradient-based models.
Scale only the target variable instead.
Trees need scaling more than neural nets do.
scenarios.why: The correct approach knows which models care: a split on 'income > 50000' is identical to 'income_scaled > 0.31' — the tree finds the same partition either way. Preprocessing stages have maintenance cost (fitted objects to version, serving parity to maintain), so each must earn its place. For trees, scaling does not.
scenarios.hint: Does the split point change when you rescale the axis?

scenarios.title: The Midnight Wrap
scenarios.situation: A model uses raw hour-of-day (0-23) to predict delivery delays. It learned that 23:00 is low-risk and 00:00 is high-risk — for the same overnight shift.
choices: The model is right — midnight is riskier than 11 PM.
Bin hours into 4 buckets: night, morning, afternoon, evening.
Circular encoding: raw hour makes 23 and 0 maximally distant though they are adjacent. Replace with sin/cos transforms (hour_sin, hour_cos) so the model sees the true adjacency.
Drop the hour feature entirely.
scenarios.why: The correct approach fixes the representation: the artifact (23 low-risk, 00 high-risk) comes from the linear encoding lying about distance, not from reality. Sin/cos encoding places adjacent hours adjacent in feature space. Coarse bucketing loses the within-bucket pattern; dropping the feature loses real signal.
scenarios.hint: How far apart are 23:00 and 00:00 — in reality vs in the encoding?
evidence: Same overnight shift split into opposite risk predictions at midnight

domains.name: ML Monitoring

scenarios.title: The Shifting Customers
scenarios.situation: Fraud model accuracy is steady, but the age feature's PSI hit 0.42 this week. A student marketing campaign launched Monday.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening and what do you do?
choices: Data drift from the campaign: the input distribution shifted (younger applicants) while the fraud relationship may still hold. Verify with delayed-label accuracy, monitor closely, and prepare a retrain on the new mix if performance degrades.
The model is broken — retrain immediately.
PSI is a vanity metric; ignore it.
Block all student applications until it settles.
scenarios.why: The correct approach interprets the signal precisely: PSI 0.42 is significant input shift with a known cause (campaign), and steady accuracy means the mapping still holds — so this is data drift to watch, not an emergency. Immediate retraining on three days of campaign data would overfit the blip; blocking applicants is a business decision disguised as ML ops.
scenarios.hint: Did the inputs change, or did the input-output relationship change?
evidence: age PSI 0.42 (was 0.08); accuracy steady; campaign launched Monday

scenarios.title: Same Inputs, New Fraud
scenarios.situation: Feature distributions are stable (all PSI < 0.1), but delayed-label fraud recall fell from 0.80 to 0.61 over two months.
scenarios.prompt: What kind of drift is this?
choices: Data drift — retrain on recent data.

Concept drift: inputs look the same but the relationship changed — fraudsters adapted their methods, so the learned mapping is stale. This needs fresh labels and likely new features capturing the new patterns, not just more of the old data.
The labels are wrong; fix the labeling.
Random fluctuation; wait another quarter.
scenarios.why: The correct approach reads the signature: stable inputs plus decaying effectiveness equals a changed relationship — the world moved, not the data pipeline. Retraining on recent data with the same features helps only if the new patterns are expressible; often concept drift demands new features or labels. A 19-point recall drop over two months is not fluctuation.
scenarios.hint: If the inputs did not change, what did?
evidence: All feature PSI < 0.1; fraud recall 0.80 -> 0.61 over 8 weeks

scenarios.title: Flying Blind
scenarios.situation: Your churn model has no ground truth for 6 months (churn is only observable at contract end). The team says monitoring is impossible until then.
choices: Nothing — monitoring without labels is impossible.
Wait 6 months, then evaluate.

Proxy signals: prediction distribution drift, feature PSI vs training baseline, and business KPIs correlated with churn (support tickets, usage drops). Log every prediction now so delayed labels can score them later.
Retrain monthly blindly to stay fresh.
scenarios.why: The correct approach refuses to fly blind: input drift (PSI) and output distribution shifts are measurable today and catch most real failures. The prediction log with request IDs makes the 6-month-later evaluation exact instead of approximate. Blind monthly retraining is motion without measurement.
scenarios.hint: What could go wrong in the next 6 months that labels would be too late to catch?
evidence: Labels available only at 6-month contract end; model serves daily

scenarios.title: The Ignored Page
scenarios.situation: The drift monitor pages the on-call 3-4 times a week for minor PSI wobbles. Last night it paged for a real accuracy collapse — nobody responded for 6 hours.
choices: The on-call engineer failed; escalate to their manager.
Drift monitoring is too sensitive; disable it.
Accuracy collapses are unpredictable; accept the 6 hours.

Alert design: noisy, unactionable pages trained the team to ignore the channel. Fix with hysteresis (2 consecutive breaches), severity tiers (ticket for drift, page for collapse), cooldowns, and action-naming alerts.
scenarios.why: The correct approach blames the system, not the human: 3-4 weekly pages for wobbles is a design that manufactures fatigue, and fatigue is why the real page died unanswered. Tiered severity routes drift to tickets and reserves pages for true emergencies; cooldowns prevent spam during investigation. The 6-hour silence was the predictable output of the alert policy.
scenarios.hint: What did the paging policy teach the team about pages?
evidence: 14 pages in 4 weeks (13 wobbles, 1 real); real page unanswered 6h

scenarios.title: Retrain on What?
scenarios.situation: The weekly retrain fired on schedule. The new model scores worse on the last-30-days holdout than the current production model.
choices: Keep the champion: the promotion gate exists for exactly this — the challenger failed to beat production on recent data, so it stays in staging. Investigate why (bad week of data? label delay?), but do not ship a worse model.
Ship it anyway — fresh models are better.
Retrain again immediately; the data must be bad.
Turn off the gate; it blocks progress.
scenarios.why: The correct approach trusts the gate over the calendar: 'retrained' is not 'improved', and the holdout comparison is the verdict. Shipping a worse model because the schedule said so is freshness theater. The investigation (was the recent data anomalous? are labels delayed?) is the real work; the gate already did its job.
scenarios.hint: What is the gate for, if not this exact situation?
evidence: Challenger holdout F1 0.81 vs champion 0.84; auto-promotion blocked

scenarios.title: The Self-Fulfilling Model
scenarios.situation: The recommender's click-through keeps rising, but user surveys show declining satisfaction. The model trains on clicks from its own rankings.
choices: The surveys are wrong; CTR is the objective truth.

Feedback loop: the model promotes items, users click what is shown, clicks train the model to promote those items — CTR rises while true satisfaction falls. Break it with exploration traffic and external satisfaction metrics.
The model needs more capacity to learn satisfaction.
Clicks are all that matter for the business.
scenarios.why: The correct approach sees the loop: the training signal (clicks) is contaminated by the model's own decisions (position bias), so rising CTR measures the loop's strength, not user happiness. Exploration traffic (randomized exposure, logged separately) reveals what users choose unprompted; surveys become the external ground truth the loop cannot bend.
scenarios.hint: Who chose the items that got the clicks — the users or the model?
evidence: CTR +22% over 6 months; satisfaction -15%; training data = own rankings' clicks

scenarios.title: The Quiet Monday
scenarios.situation: No alerts fired all quarter. The model's business KPI drifted down 12%. Monitoring dashboards are all green.
scenarios.prompt: What does this tell you about the monitoring?
choices: The KPI drop is unrelated to the model.
Green dashboards prove the model is fine.

It monitors the wrong things: green dashboards alongside declining KPIs mean the tracked metrics (uptime, latency, input PSI) missed the failure mode — likely concept drift or a broken business assumption. Add KPI-linked and delayed-label metrics.
More dashboards are needed.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats the KPI as the ultimate monitor: infrastructure metrics being green while the outcome decays means observability has a blind spot exactly where it matters. The fix is metric design — tie monitoring to the business outcome via delayed labels and proxy KPIs — not more of the same green lights.
scenarios.hint: What is the model FOR, and is that being measured?
objectives: Monitor the outcome, not just the machinery
evidence: All infra/drift dashboards green; business KPI -12% in a quarter
