scenarios.title: Works on My Machine
scenarios.situation: The model API runs perfectly on the data scientist's laptop but crashes in production with dependency conflicts.
choices: Containerize with pinned dependencies: a Docker image carrying the exact Python version, pinned requirements, and the versioned model artifact runs identically everywhere — the environment becomes part of the artifact.
Install the laptop's exact packages on the prod server by hand.
Tell the data scientist to use the prod server's Python version.
Rewrite the API to avoid the conflicting packages.
scenarios.why: The correct approach eliminates the environment as a variable: the container is the deployment unit, built once and run anywhere. Hand-syncing packages is fragile archaeology; matching the laptop to prod inverts the responsibility; rewriting around conflicts dodges today's issue only.
scenarios.hint: What differs between the two environments — and should it be allowed to?
objectives: Make env part of the artifact
evidence: Identical code+model: works on laptop, ImportError in prod

scenarios.title: The Friday Swap
scenarios.situation: A new model version must go live today. It is a major architecture change, and offline eval looks good.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safest release plan?
choices: Deploy 100% now — offline eval is good and today is the deadline.

Shadow first, then canary: run the new architecture on live traffic without serving its answers to catch real-world surprises, then ramp 5% → 25% → 100% with metric checks — rollback stays one routing flip away.
Deploy 100% but watch the dashboards closely.
Delay until Monday, then deploy 100%.
scenarios.why: The correct approach scales caution with risk: architecture changes carry the highest surprise potential, so shadow mode buys real-world evidence at zero user risk before any traffic ramps. Big-bang deploys convert deadline pressure into incident risk; watching dashboards during a 100% swap is damage observation, not control.
scenarios.hint: What could live traffic contain that offline eval never saw?
evidence: Architecture swap, offline +2 F1, release due today

scenarios.title: The $12,000 Surprise
scenarios.situation: The monthly cloud bill shows $12,000 for GPU serving. The workload is a nightly batch job someone deployed as an always-on API 'temporarily' 4 months ago.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix and the prevention?
choices: Negotiate a discount with the cloud provider.
The batch job is important; $12k is the cost of doing business.
Move to scheduled batch on spot instances (dollars per day instead of hundreds), and add spend alerts plus monthly top-cost reviews so 'temporary' never compounds silently again.
Turn it off entirely.
scenarios.why: The correct approach attacks both the waste and the process: batch-on-spot matches cost to the actual need (scheduled, latency-insensitive), cutting the bill ~18x, while spend alerts and cost reviews catch the next 'temporary' deployment in week one instead of month four. Discounts trim the symptom; acceptance institutionalizes the waste.
scenarios.hint: What serving mode does a nightly batch actually need?
evidence: $12k/month GPU serving for a nightly batch job

scenarios.title: The 2 GB Commit
scenarios.situation: Someone committed a 2 GB model file to git. Clones now take 20 minutes and the repo is unusable.
choices: Use git LFS for the model file.
Split the model into smaller commits.
It is fine — storage is cheap.
Models live in artifact storage (versioned model registry / object store), never in git: git tracks code, the registry tracks large binaries with lineage — reference the version, not the bytes.
scenarios.why: The correct approach separates concerns: git is for diffable code, artifact stores are for large versioned binaries with metadata and lineage. LFS papers over the problem while keeping binaries in the code workflow; smaller commits multiply the pain. The registry gives you versions, stages, and provenance that git cannot.
scenarios.hint: What is git good at — and is a 2 GB binary it?
evidence: 2 GB model.pkl committed; clone time 20 min; team blocked

scenarios.title: The Three-Hour Build
scenarios.situation: Every commit triggers full model training in CI: builds take 3 hours, so engineers skip CI with --no-verify.
choices: Tier the CI: fast tests (unit, schema, lint) on every commit in minutes; slow tests (1%-data training smoke, eval gate) nightly and pre-merge. CI people bypass is CI that does not exist.
Buy more CI runners to make 3-hour builds faster.
Remove CI entirely; it is slowing the team down.
Train on even more data in CI for better gates.
scenarios.why: The correct approach respects the feedback loop: per-commit CI must answer in minutes, or humans route around it — and a bypassed gate protects nothing. The training smoke on 1% data catches pipeline breakage cheaply; the full eval gate runs where its cost is amortized. Fast feedback first, thoroughness on schedule.
scenarios.hint: What is the CI actually optimizing for — thoroughness or compliance?
evidence: Full training per commit: 3h builds; engineers routinely skip with --no-verify

scenarios.title: Wrong at Scale
scenarios.situation: The new model version is serving nonsense predictions to 100% of traffic. It has been live for 40 minutes while the team investigates the cause.
scenarios.prompt: What should have happened in the first 60 seconds?
choices: Keep investigating; rolling back might lose the evidence.

Route traffic back to the previous version immediately — containment before diagnosis. The old version is one routing flip away; every minute of investigation-first is a minute of wrong answers at scale.
Wait for the on-call ML engineer to wake up.
Scale up replicas to handle the load.
scenarios.why: The correct approach separates containment from diagnosis: rollback restores correct behavior in seconds and preserves all the logs needed for diagnosis afterward. Investigating while bad predictions serve trades user harm for zero diagnostic benefit — the evidence is in the logs either way.
scenarios.hint: What is the cost of each additional minute before rollback?
evidence: v5 serving bad predictions to 100% traffic for 40 min; v4 available

scenarios.title: The Late Data
scenarios.situation: The retraining pipeline failed silently for 2 weeks because the upstream data export moved from 6 AM to 9 AM and the pipeline runs at 7 AM on stale-or-missing data.
choices: Move the pipeline to 10 AM.
Ask upstream never to change their schedule.

Event-driven triggering with data contracts: the pipeline waits for the upstream 'data ready' event (not the clock) and validates freshness on arrival — schedule assumptions become explicit dependencies.
Check manually each morning that data arrived.
scenarios.why: The correct approach replaces clock coupling with event coupling: triggering on the upstream completion event plus a freshness validation means schedule changes propagate correctly instead of silently starving the pipeline. Moving to 10 AM just moves the fragility; upstream will change again; manual checks are the pre-automation habit.
scenarios.hint: What is the pipeline actually waiting for — 7 AM, or the data?
evidence: Pipeline ran 14 days on missing data; no failure alert fired

lessons.title: AI Lab: Engineering Around the Model — Core concepts
concepts: The model is one folder: weights, tokenizer, config. The product is the scaffolding around it — prompt pipeline, tools, memory, sandbox, tests, traces.
Local inference is an economics decision: trade API bills and data egress for capital cost and operational burden; quantization (notably the GGUF format) sets the exchange rate.
Match the runtime tier to the job: llama.cpp/Ollama at the runtime layer, LM Studio/Jan on the desktop, Open WebUI in the browser — and vLLM only as a production serving stack for operators.

The agent loop is one operations loop: request → agent → memory → tools → runtime → eval → retry → deploy. Frameworks, memory systems, sandboxed execution, evals, and observability are each a layer with its own failure modes.

Generation must be separated from verification: a main writer for momentum, a silent advisor reviewing at three trigger points, specialist subagents dividing labor, a cheap router protecting the expensive model's attention.
Memory is not one thing: persistent vector memory and temporal knowledge graphs answer different questions — store retrievable facts in one, evolving relationships in the other.
Evals prove the agent passed the evals. LLM-as-judge inherits judge bias; small suites miss the long tail; the honest question is always 'what would this eval miss?'

example.code:
ollama pull llama3.1:8b
ollama run llama3.1:8b "Summarize the local-vs-API tradeoff in one sentence."
# Query the same model over HTTP like a product would:
curl -s http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d '{"model":"llama3.1:8b","prompt":"What is quantization?","stream":false}' | python3 -c "import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['response'])"
example.walkthrough: Pull an open-weight model, run it interactively, then hit the same model over its local HTTP API — the exact shape a product's request path takes. Notice the third step needs no new model: the 'product' is the API wrapper, the prompt pipeline, and whatever you build around the response.

pitfalls: Common trap: 'Open weights means open source.' The artifact is open; the license governs use, and licenses range from permissive to research-only to commercial-restricted. Read the model card.
Common trap: 'Local means private.' Privacy is a property of the whole data path — telemetry-phoning UIs and cloud-synced clients void it.
Common trap: treating vLLM as a desktop tool. It is a serving stack for operators; on a laptop it is operational weight without the workload.

Common trap: upgrading the model while neglecting the scaffolding. Past a capability floor, product quality is dominated by retrieval quality, tool design, eval coverage, and the review loop — a smarter engine in the same broken car.
