lessons.title: NumPy: Thinking in Arrays
concepts: NumPy arrays are the lingua franca of machine learning: fixed-type, contiguous memory blocks that run numeric code orders of magnitude faster than Python loops
Broadcasting lets operations combine mismatched shapes without explicit loops — a (3,1) array plus a (4,) array yields a (3,4) result
Vectorization replaces slow Python for-loops: np.sum((a - b) ** 2) computes squared distance over whole arrays at C speed
When array code misbehaves, check shape and dtype first: print(a.shape, a.dtype) before anything else — most bugs live there

example.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]], dtype=np.float64)
print(a.shape)        # (2, 2)
print(a.mean(axis=0)) # column means: [2. 3.]
print(a @ a.T)        # matrix multiply with transpose
example.walkthrough: The example builds a 2x2 float array. a.shape reports (2,2); a.mean(axis=0) averages down each column to [2, 3]; a @ a.T is matrix multiplication, the core operation inside every neural network layer. A practical use: the Euclidean distance between two feature vectors x and y is np.sqrt(np.sum((x - y) ** 2)) — one line, no loops, and fast enough to run over millions of rows.

pitfalls: Writing Python for-loops over array rows — 100x slower than the vectorized form and the most common beginner bottleneck
Ignoring dtype: float64 arrays use twice the memory of float32, which matters enormously for embeddings and GPU work
Confusing elementwise * with matrix @ — they are completely different operations with silently different shapes
lessons.try_it: Create two 1000-element arrays and time a loop-based dot product versus np.dot. Record the speedup.

lessons.title: Pandas: Data Wrangling for ML
concepts: DataFrames are labeled 2D tables: df['col'] selects a column, df.loc[] selects by label, df.iloc[] by position — mixing them up is the classic pandas bug
groupby() is the workhorse of exploratory analysis: df.groupby('segment')['revenue'].mean() answers 'which segment performs best' in one line
Missing data must be handled deliberately: df.isna().sum() audits it, then fillna(), dropna(), or model-based imputation — never ignore it silently
Vectorized column ops beat row iteration: df['total'] = df['price'] * df['qty'] runs at C speed; df.iterrows() does not

example.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('customers.csv')
print(df.isna().sum())          # audit missing values
med = df['age'].median()
df['age'] = df['age'].fillna(med)  # impute with median
print(df.groupby('tier')['spend'].mean())
example.walkthrough: This snippet loads customer data, audits missing values per column, and fills missing ages with the median (robust to outliers, unlike the mean). The groupby then computes average spend per tier. The walkthrough pattern is always: load, audit (shape, dtypes, missing), clean, then aggregate — skipping the audit step is how bad data silently poisons models.

pitfalls: Chained assignment df[df.x>0]['y']=1 triggers SettingWithCopyWarning and may silently fail — always use df.loc[mask, 'y'] = 1
Calling fillna with the mean on skewed data — the median is usually the safer default imputation
Forgetting that groupby drops NaN keys silently — missing segments vanish from your aggregates
lessons.try_it: Load any CSV you have, run isna().sum() and describe(), and write one sentence about data quality.

lessons.title: Pythonic ML Code: Comprehensions, Generators, Typing
concepts: List comprehensions replace map/filter loops: [clean(t) for t in texts if t] is faster to read and write than the equivalent for-loop
Generators stream data without loading it all: (row for row in open('big.csv')) processes arbitrarily large files in constant memory
Type hints (def train(X: np.ndarray) -> float:) catch shape and type bugs at edit time and document interfaces for teammates
Dataclasses make experiment configs explicit: @dataclass class Config with lr, batch_size, epochs beats a dict of magic strings

example.walkthrough: The dataclass turns scattered hyperparameters into one typed, inspectable object you can log in full at the start of every run — this is the seed of experiment tracking. The batches() generator yields mini-batches lazily instead of building a giant list, the same pattern PyTorch DataLoaders use internally. Type hints on both make misuse visible immediately.

pitfalls: Building giant intermediate lists when a generator would do — the classic out-of-memory on large datasets
Untyped function signatures in shared ML code — every caller guesses at expected shapes
Magic numbers scattered through training scripts — centralize them in a config object
lessons.try_it: Convert one of your training scripts' hyperparameters into a dataclass and log it at run start.

lessons.title: Reproducibility: Envs, Seeds, and Requirements
concepts: 'Works on my machine' kills ML projects: pin every dependency (pip freeze > requirements.txt) so training reruns identically anywhere
Randomness must be seeded everywhere it hides: Python random, NumPy, and any framework (torch.manual_seed) — one unseeded source breaks reproducibility
Virtual environments (venv/conda) isolate project dependencies; never install ML packages into the system Python
Log the environment with the experiment: Python version, package versions, git commit hash, and dataset hash alongside every result

example.code:
import random, numpy as np
SEED = 42
random.seed(SEED)
np.random.seed(SEED)
# torch.manual_seed(SEED)  # uncomment for PyTorch
# torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)  # slower but exact
example.walkthrough: Setting the same seed in every randomness source makes shuffles, initializations, and sampling deterministic, so a run can be replayed exactly. This snippet is the first five lines of every serious training script. Combined with pinned requirements and a logged git hash, it turns 'I got 94% once' into a result anyone can reproduce — the difference between a demo and engineering.

pitfalls: Seeding only NumPy while the framework samples unseeded — partial seeding gives false confidence
Unpinned requirements.txt — 'numpy' without a version means a different numpy six months from now
No git commit recorded with results — you cannot diff what you cannot identify
lessons.try_it: Add full seeding plus a requirements freeze to your current project and verify two runs match.

lessons.title: Anatomy of an ML Pipeline
concepts: A pipeline is a DAG of stages: ingest, validate, transform, train, evaluate, register, serve — each stage has explicit inputs, outputs, and contracts
Thinking in DAGs (directed acyclic graphs) forces you to declare dependencies: the train stage cannot run before validation passes
Every stage should be idempotent: rerunning it with the same inputs produces the same outputs — this is what makes pipelines debuggable
Fail fast and loudly: schema checks at ingest catch corrupt data in seconds instead of after a 6-hour training run

example.code:
stages = ['ingest', 'validate', 'transform', 'train', 'evaluate', 'register', 'serve']
# each stage: run(inputs) -> (outputs, metadata)
# validate() raises on schema drift -> train never sees bad data
example.walkthrough: Each stage is a function with declared inputs and outputs plus metadata (row counts, hashes, timestamps). The validate stage is the gatekeeper: it checks schemas, ranges, and null rates, and raises before training wastes GPU hours. Idempotency means you can rerun any single stage after fixing it without redoing upstream work — the property that makes a pipeline operable instead of fragile.

pitfalls: A notebook with cells run out of order — hidden state makes it unreproducible by anyone including future-you
No validation stage — corrupt upstream data trains silently into a bad model
Stages that depend on execution order instead of declared inputs — reruns produce different results
lessons.try_it: Sketch the 7-stage DAG for a project you know, naming each stage's inputs and outputs.

lessons.title: sklearn Pipelines: No Leakage by Construction
concepts: sklearn's Pipeline chains transformers and a final estimator so preprocessing and modeling are one object: fit, predict, and cross-validate apply to the whole chain
ColumnTransformer applies different preprocessing per column type: scaling for numerics, one-hot for categoricals — declared once, applied consistently
Pipelines prevent target leakage structurally: transformers fit only on training folds during cross-validation, never on the full dataset
The fitted pipeline IS the deployable artifact: pickle the whole pipeline and serving automatically applies identical preprocessing

example.code:
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

pipe = Pipeline([
    ('prep', ColumnTransformer([
        ('num', StandardScaler(), num_cols),
        ('cat', OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore'), cat_cols)])),
    ('clf', LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)  # prep fits ONLY on train
example.walkthrough: The ColumnTransformer declares per-type preprocessing; the Pipeline glues it to the classifier. Calling pipe.fit(X_train, y_train) fits the scaler and encoder on training data only — during cross_val_score(pipe, X, y), each fold refits preprocessing on its own training split. Pickling pipe gives you a single artifact that transforms raw features exactly as training did, eliminating training-serving skew.

pitfalls: Fitting the scaler on the full dataset before splitting — test statistics leak into training through the scaler
Reimplementing preprocessing separately at serving time — drift between the two implementations is inevitable
Forgetting handle_unknown='ignore' — new categories at serving time crash the encoder
lessons.try_it: Refactor one of your notebooks' preprocessing into a Pipeline and verify cross_val_score still works.

lessons.title: Data Versioning and Lineage
concepts: Models are functions of their training data: if you cannot name the exact dataset version behind a model, you cannot reproduce, audit, or roll back that model
Hash every dataset (SHA-256 of the file or a content hash of the query+timestamp) and log the hash with each experiment — cheap and decisive
Data versioning tools track which data produced which model, so a data bug can be traced forward to every affected model
Lineage answers 'why did the model change?': the diff between dataset v3 and v4 explains the accuracy delta

example.code:
# dataset manifest written at training time
dataset = {'name': 'churn', 'version': 'v4',
           'sha256': '9f2c...', 'rows': 48210,
           'query': 'SELECT ... WHERE dt <= 2026-10-01'}
# log dataset['sha256'] with every experiment
example.walkthrough: The manifest pins the dataset exactly: name, version tag, content hash, row count, and the query that produced it. When accuracy drops after a retrain, you diff the manifests first — v4 added 3,000 rows from a new source, and there is your explanation. Without the hash, you are guessing whether the data or the code changed.

pitfalls: 'data/final_v2_REAL.csv' naming — filenames are not versioning and 'final' is a lie
Logging model metrics without the dataset hash — the result is uninterpretable later
Retraining on 'whatever is in the folder now' — silent data changes become silent model changes
lessons.try_it: Hash your current training dataset and add the hash to your experiment log today.

lessons.title: Orchestration: Scheduling the Machine
concepts: Orchestration turns a pipeline into a system: scheduled runs, dependency handling, retries, and alerting — the pipeline runs itself
DAG schedulers express 'retrain weekly, but only if fresh data validated' as code: each stage is a task with upstream dependencies
Retries with backoff handle transient failures (flaky APIs, spot preemptions); permanent failures page a human with the failed stage's logs
Backfills rerun historical windows through the current pipeline — essential when you fix a bug and need corrected features for past dates

example.code:
# conceptual DAG (Airflow-style)
with DAG('churn_retrain', schedule='@weekly') as dag:
    raw = ingest()          # task 1
    ok = validate(raw)      # task 2, depends on 1
    feats = transform(ok)   # task 3, depends on 2
    model = train(feats)    # task 4, depends on 3
    # failures retry 3x, then alert
example.walkthrough: Each task declares its dependencies, so the scheduler runs ingest, then validate, then transform, then train — skipping downstream tasks if validation fails. The weekly schedule plus retry policy means retraining happens without human babysitting, and failures arrive as alerts naming the exact failed stage instead of a mysterious stale model.

pitfalls: Cron jobs with no dependency handling — train runs on stale data when ingest fails silently
No retries — one transient network blip kills the weekly retrain
Manual retraining 'when someone remembers' — models silently go stale for months
lessons.try_it: Write the task list and dependencies for retraining one of your models on a schedule.

lessons.title: Train, Validation, Test: The Three-Way Split
concepts: Three splits, three jobs: train fits parameters, validation selects hyperparameters and early-stops, test estimates real-world performance exactly once
The test set is sacred: touch it during development and your performance estimate is optimistic fiction — lock it away until the end
Stratify splits on imbalanced targets so each split mirrors the class distribution; random splits can starve small classes
Time-ordered data needs time-based splits (train on past, validate/test on future) — random shuffling leaks the future into training

example.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
X_tr, X_tmp, y_tr, y_tmp = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.4, stratify=y, random_state=42)
X_va, X_te, y_va, y_te = train_test_split(X_tmp, y_tmp, test_size=0.5, stratify=y_tmp, random_state=42)
# 60% train / 20% val / 20% test
example.walkthrough: The double split yields 60/20/40... precisely 60% train, 20% validation, 20% test, stratified so each split keeps the class balance. random_state makes the split reproducible. The discipline: tune everything against validation, and evaluate on test once — if you iterate against test, it becomes validation by another name and your final number lies.

pitfalls: Tuning hyperparameters against the test set — the most common way to publish inflated numbers
Random splits on time-series data — the model 'predicts' the past using the future
Tiny validation sets — hyperparameter choices become noise; keep val/test at 15-20%+ each
lessons.try_it: Check your current project: which split did you last tune against? Fix it if the answer is test.

lessons.title: Loss Functions and Gradient Descent
concepts: The loss function is the model's scorecard: MSE for regression penalizes large errors quadratically; cross-entropy for classification penalizes confident wrongness
Gradient descent walks downhill on the loss surface: learning rate controls step size — too small crawls, too large diverges
Loss curves are diagnostic instruments: smooth decrease is healthy; oscillation means lower the learning rate; flatlining means raise it or check the data
The optimizer (SGD, Adam) is the walking strategy; the loss is the terrain — tune the learning rate before anything else

example.code:
for epoch in range(epochs):
    preds = model(X_train)          # forward pass
    loss = cross_entropy(preds, y)  # scorecard
    loss.backward()                 # gradients: which way is down?
    optimizer.step()                # take the step
    optimizer.zero_grad()           # reset for next batch
example.walkthrough: Each epoch: predict, score with the loss, compute gradients (the direction of steepest descent), step the weights, reset gradients. Watch the loss curve: if it explodes to NaN, the learning rate is too high; if it barely moves after epochs, it is too low or the features need scaling. This loop is the engine inside every neural network trainer.

pitfalls: Default learning rate worship — the single most impactful hyperparameter, yet often left untouched
Judging training by accuracy alone — the loss curve tells you about optimization health; accuracy tells you about the task
Ignoring NaN losses — a NaN is never 'just noise'; it means divergence, overflow, or bad data
lessons.try_it: Plot your last training run's loss curve and diagnose it: healthy, oscillating, or flatlined?

lessons.title: Overfitting vs Underfitting
concepts: Overfitting memorizes noise: training accuracy soars while validation stalls or drops — the model learned the training set, not the problem
Underfitting learns too little: both train and validation accuracy are poor — the model lacks capacity or the features lack signal
Learning curves diagnose: plot train vs validation score against training size — a persistent gap screams overfitting; both low screams underfitting
Regularization (L1/L2, dropout, early stopping) constrains memorization; more data and better features cure underfitting

example.code:
# diagnosing from scores
train_acc, val_acc = 0.99, 0.71  # big gap -> overfitting
# fixes: more data, regularization, simpler model, early stopping
train_acc, val_acc = 0.68, 0.66  # both low -> underfitting
# fixes: more capacity, better features, train longer
example.walkthrough: A 28-point train/validation gap is textbook overfitting: the model has capacity to memorize and is doing exactly that. Fixes in order of leverage: more training data, stronger regularization, simpler model, early stopping on validation loss. When both scores are low and close, the model is underfitting — give it more capacity or better features, not regularization.

pitfalls: 'Fixing' overfitting by collecting test-set-like data — that is leakage, not a fix
Regularizing an underfit model — constraints on a model that already cannot learn
Judging fit from training accuracy alone — the gap is the diagnosis, not the absolute number
lessons.try_it: Plot learning curves for your current model and classify it: overfit, underfit, or just right?

lessons.title: Hyperparameter Tuning That Works
concepts: Tune in order of impact: learning rate first, then architecture/capacity, then regularization — tuning batch size before learning rate wastes runs
Random search beats grid search: it explores more distinct values of the important parameters for the same budget
Budget your search: a few dozen random trials with early stopping beats exhaustive grids that take weeks
Log every trial's full config and score — tuning without a search history is just guessing with extra steps

example.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
from scipy.stats import loguniform
search = RandomizedSearchCV(pipe,
    {'clf__C': loguniform(1e-3, 1e3)},
    n_iter=30, cv=5, scoring='f1', random_state=42)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)  # tunes on CV, never touches test
example.walkthrough: RandomizedSearchCV samples 30 values of C from a log-uniform distribution (covering orders of magnitude, which is how regularization strength behaves), evaluates each with 5-fold CV on the training data, and scores by F1 — the right metric for the imbalanced problem at hand. The test set stays locked. Thirty smart trials beat a 1,000-point grid that wastes 97% of its budget on irrelevant combinations.

pitfalls: Grid-searching everything including irrelevant parameters — budget burned on noise
Tuning on the test set — every 'improvement' is partially fiction
No search history logged — you cannot learn what worked across projects
lessons.try_it: Run a 20-trial random search on one model, log all trials, and note which parameter mattered most.

lessons.title: Batch vs Online Inference
concepts: Online inference serves one request at a time with millisecond latency budgets — think fraud scoring during checkout
Batch inference scores millions of rows on a schedule with no latency pressure — think nightly churn predictions
Throughput vs latency: batch maximizes predictions per dollar, online minimizes milliseconds per prediction — optimize for the right one
Choose by need: if the decision can wait hours, batch is 10-100x cheaper; if a user is waiting, you need online

example.walkthrough: A fraud model blocking checkout must answer in under 100ms — that is online inference behind an API with warm replicas. A churn model emailing at-risk customers nightly is batch: a scheduled job scores the whole customer table once. Running the churn job as an online API wastes money on idle replicas; running fraud as a nightly batch misses the fraud. Match the serving mode to the decision latency.

pitfalls: Online serving for batchable workloads — paying for idle GPUs to score nightly jobs
Batch for real-time needs — the prediction arrives after the decision was made
No latency budget defined — 'fast enough' is not an SLO you can engineer to
lessons.try_it: Classify three models you know as batch or online, and state each one's latency budget.

lessons.title: Building a Prediction API
concepts: A prediction API is a contract: POST /predict accepts validated JSON, returns predictions plus model version — nothing more
Validate inputs at the boundary: schema checks (types, ranges, required fields) turn garbage-in crashes into clean 400 errors
Load the model once at startup, not per request — per-request loading turns millisecond inference into second-long cold calls
Return the model version with every prediction: when debugging, 'which model said this?' must be answerable from the response alone

example.walkthrough: The model loads once when the app starts, so requests never pay load cost. Each request validates the feature dict against a schema, scores with the preloaded model, and returns both the probability and the model version. That version field is the cheapest debugging tool you own: when a prediction looks wrong next month, the response tells you exactly which model produced it.

pitfalls: Loading the model inside the request handler — latency explodes and memory leaks follow
No input validation — one malformed request crashes the worker for everyone
Returning raw numpy types — they are not JSON serializable; cast to float
lessons.try_it: Sketch the /predict contract (inputs, outputs, errors) for one of your models.

lessons.title: Latency Budgets and Optimization
concepts: A latency budget decomposes end-to-end time: network + deserialization + preprocessing + inference + serialization — measure each slice before optimizing
Dynamic batching groups concurrent requests into one model call: 32 requests in one batch cost barely more than one alone on a GPU
Caching repeated inputs (same user, same features) can eliminate inference entirely for hot keys — check hit rate before building it
Quantization (fp32 to int8) shrinks models 4x and speeds CPU inference 2-4x, with small accuracy cost — measure the tradeoff on your data

example.code:
# finding the slow slice (pseudo-timers)
with timer('preprocess'): x = prep(raw)
with timer('inference'):  p = model.predict(x)
with timer('total'):      ...
# optimize the biggest slice first, not the easiest
example.walkthrough: If p99 is 800ms against a 200ms budget, timers might show inference at 600ms and preprocessing at 150ms — the model is the target, not the JSON parsing. Dynamic batching could cut inference to 80ms by grouping 16 concurrent requests. Without the breakdown you would 'optimize' serialization for a 5ms win while the real problem laughs at you.

pitfalls: Optimizing before measuring — the classic premature optimization, now with GPUs
Quantizing without re-measuring accuracy — speed means nothing if quality collapses
Ignoring preprocessing — it is frequently slower than the model itself
lessons.try_it: Instrument one inference path with timers and name the biggest slice.

lessons.title: Scaling Model Serving
concepts: Scale replicas, not model size: N identical containers behind a load balancer handle N times the traffic with no code changes
Autoscaling on the right signal: queue depth or p99 latency, not CPU — inference bottlenecks show up in latency first
Separate the API from the model worker when traffic is bursty: a queue between them absorbs spikes without dropping requests
Load test before launch: ramp to 2x expected peak and watch p99, error rate, and memory — production is a bad place to discover limits

example.walkthrough: The policy scales on p99 latency — the user-facing signal — with a cooldown to avoid flapping, and never below 2 replicas so one failure does not take you down. The API/worker split with a queue means a 10x traffic spike waits in line instead of timing out. Load testing at 2x peak finds the breaking point on your schedule, not the users'.

pitfalls: Autoscaling on CPU for GPU-bound inference — the signal never fires while users suffer
Single replica in production — every deploy and every crash is downtime
No load test — 'it worked in staging' with 1% of production traffic
lessons.try_it: Write the autoscale policy (metric, thresholds, min replicas) for one of your APIs.

lessons.title: Serving Reliability: Health, Warmup, Rollback
concepts: Health endpoints (/health) must verify the model actually loads and predicts — a 200 from a broken model is worse than a 500
Warmup requests on startup prime caches and GPU memory so the first real user does not pay cold-start latency
Versioned deployments (v4 and v5 side by side) make rollback a routing change, not a redeploy — rollback in seconds, not minutes
Shadow mode runs the new model on live traffic without serving its answers: real-world validation with zero user risk

example.code:
# startup sequence
model = load('model_v5.pkl')
warmup_batch = load_sample_inputs()
model.predict(warmup_batch)  # prime GPU, caches
assert health_check(model)   # predict on canary input, verify sane output
example.walkthrough: The startup sequence loads v5, runs a warmup batch through it (filling GPU memory and caches), then asserts a health check: predict on a known input and verify the output is sane. Only then does the replica join the load balancer. With v4 still routed as primary, flipping to v5 — or back — is a config change measured in seconds.

pitfalls: Health check that only pings the web server — the API is 'up' while the model is broken
No warmup — first users after each deploy eat multi-second cold starts
In-place model swaps with no rollback path — a bad model means a bad hour
lessons.try_it: Add a real model health check (predict + sanity assert) to one of your services.

lessons.title: Embeddings: Meaning as Coordinates
concepts: Embeddings turn text into dense vectors where semantic similarity becomes geometric closeness — 'king' minus 'man' plus 'woman' lands near 'queen'
Cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors, ignoring magnitude: ideal for text where document length should not dominate
Embedding models are interchangeable parts with incompatible outputs: vectors from model A cannot be compared with vectors from model B
Dimension is a cost knob: 768-dim vectors cost 3x the memory and compute of 256-dim — benchmark whether the quality delta justifies it

example.walkthrough: Cosine similarity divides the dot product by both magnitudes, leaving pure directional agreement between -1 and 1. The example scores ~0.994 for nearly parallel vectors — near-identical meaning. In practice you embed a query and a corpus, rank by this score, and the top-k are your semantically closest documents. The model-A/model-B incompatibility is the trap: re-embed the whole corpus when you switch models, or your index is garbage.

pitfalls: Comparing vectors across different embedding models — the coordinates live in different spaces
Using Euclidean distance on unnormalized embeddings when length varies — cosine exists for this reason
Assuming bigger dimensions always win — measure quality per dollar, not per dimension
lessons.try_it: Compute cosine similarity by hand for [1,0] and [1,1], then verify with the function.

lessons.title: Chunking: The Unit of Retrieval
concepts: RAG retrieves chunks, not documents: chunk size sets the granularity of what the generator sees — too big dilutes, too small fragments
Overlap (10-20%) between consecutive chunks preserves context across boundaries so ideas split mid-chunk still resolve
Chunk by structure when you can: paragraphs, sections, or semantic boundaries beat naive fixed-size splits
Metadata per chunk (source, page, date) turns retrieved text into citable evidence instead of anonymous snippets

example.code:
# naive vs structural
naive = [text[i:i+500] for i in range(0, len(text), 400)]  # 500 chars, 100 overlap
# better: split on paragraph boundaries, then pack to ~500 chars
example.walkthrough: The naive splitter cuts every 500 characters with 100 characters of overlap, so a sentence split across the boundary still appears whole in one chunk. Structural chunking goes further: split on paragraphs first, then pack paragraphs into ~500-char chunks — ideas stay intact. Either way, attach metadata (document title, section, page) to each chunk so retrieved results can cite their sources.

pitfalls: One giant chunk per document — retrieval returns the whole haystack with the needle
Zero overlap — the key sentence is always the one that got split
No metadata on chunks — retrieved text cannot be cited or filtered
lessons.try_it: Chunk a real document two ways (fixed-size vs paragraph-aware) and compare retrieval quality.

lessons.title: Vector Search: From Exact to Approximate
concepts: Exact search compares the query against every vector: perfect recall, but O(n) per query — dead at 10M+ vectors
Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes trade a little recall for 100x+ speed: HNSW graphs and IVF partitions are the workhorses
Recall@k measures what ANN gives up: what fraction of the true top-k the index actually returns — tune the index until recall@k meets your bar
Hybrid search (vector + keyword/BM25) beats pure vector on exact-term queries like product codes and names

example.code:
# exact (fine at small scale)
scores = X @ q  # cosine if normalized
topk = np.argsort(scores)[-5:][::-1]
# ANN (at scale): build HNSW index once, query in ms
example.walkthrough: With normalized vectors, cosine similarity is just a matrix multiply: X @ q scores the whole corpus, argsort takes the top 5. This is exact and perfect — until the corpus hits millions and each query scans gigabytes. ANN indexes (HNSW) pre-organize vectors into navigable graphs so queries traverse a tiny fraction, returning in milliseconds at 95%+ recall.

pitfalls: Exact search at 50M vectors — latency measured in seconds, users measured in departures
ANN with untuned recall — fast wrong answers are still wrong answers
Pure vector search for SKU lookups — embeddings mangle exact codes; add keyword search
lessons.try_it: Benchmark exact vs ANN retrieval time and recall@10 on 100k vectors.

lessons.title: RAG Architecture: Retrieve, Augment, Generate
concepts: RAG grounds generation in retrieved evidence: the retriever finds relevant chunks, the prompt includes them, the generator answers from them — hallucinations drop because the facts are in context
The pipeline has three failure points: retrieval misses (wrong chunks), context overflow (too many chunks), generation ignores context — instrument each separately
Top-k is a tuning knob: k=3 is precise but thin, k=10 is rich but noisy — evaluate answer quality across k on real questions
Evaluation needs ground truth: a set of questions with known answers, scored for correctness and citation fidelity

example.code:
# RAG skeleton
chunks = retriever.search(query, k=5)      # 1. retrieve
context = '\n'.join(c.text for c in chunks)  # 2. assemble
prompt = f'Answer using ONLY this context:\n{context}\nQ: {query}'
answer = llm.generate(prompt)                 # 3. generate
example.walkthrough: The retriever fetches the 5 most similar chunks; they are concatenated as the context; the prompt instructs the model to answer only from that context. When the answer hallucinates, the skeleton tells you where to look: check whether the right chunks were retrieved (retrieval problem) or retrieved but ignored (generation problem). 'Answer using ONLY this context' is the single highest-leverage prompt line in RAG.

pitfalls: Blaming the LLM for retrieval failures — if the chunks are wrong, no prompt fixes the answer
k=50 'to be safe' — context noise drowns the signal and explodes cost
No eval set — 'it feels better' is not a measurement
lessons.try_it: Build the skeleton above on 20 documents and test 5 questions end to end.

lessons.title: Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Retrieval
concepts: Metadata filters (date, source, department) shrink the search space before vector ranking — precision up, cost down
Filter-then-rank beats rank-then-filter: applying the date filter first means the vector search only considers eligible chunks
Hybrid retrieval fuses dense vectors (meaning) with sparse BM25 (exact terms): reciprocal rank fusion combines both ranked lists
Access control belongs in the filter: never retrieve chunks the user is not allowed to see, no matter how similar

example.code:
# filtered search
cands = index.search(query_vec, k=50)          # vector candidates
cands = [c for c in cands if c.meta['dept'] == user.dept]  # hard filter
kw = bm25.search(query, k=50)                  # keyword candidates
final = rrf_fuse(cands, kw)[:5]                # fused top-5
example.walkthrough: The vector search returns 50 candidates; the department filter drops anything the user cannot access; BM25 contributes exact-term matches the embeddings might miss; reciprocal rank fusion merges both lists into a final top 5. The access-control filter is load-bearing: similarity must never override authorization — filter first, rank second.

pitfalls: Post-filtering after top-k — the 5 best chunks get filtered to 2 and quality collapses
No access filtering — the retriever happily returns restricted documents to anyone
Pure dense search on part numbers — 'XJ-4471' retrieves 'XJ-4472' as 'similar'
lessons.try_it: Add a department filter to your retriever and verify restricted chunks never surface.

lessons.title: Why GPUs Win at Machine Learning
concepts: GPUs are throughput monsters: thousands of small cores executing the same operation on different data — exactly what matrix math needs
The win is parallelism plus memory bandwidth: a GPU moves data to its cores 10-20x faster than a CPU moves data to its cores
Not everything belongs on GPU: small models, tiny batches, and latency-sensitive single requests often run faster on CPU (no transfer overhead)
Utilization is the metric: a GPU at 15% utilization is an expensive space heater — profile before renting bigger iron

example.code:
# where the time goes
# CPU->GPU transfer: 2ms | GPU compute: 0.5ms | GPU->CPU: 2ms
# tiny batch: transfer dominates -> CPU wins
# large batch: compute dominates -> GPU wins big
example.walkthrough: For a tiny batch, most wall-clock time is PCIe transfer, not computation — the GPU's speed never gets used and the CPU (zero transfer) wins. Scale the batch up and compute dominates, letting thousands of cores amortize the transfer. The lesson: benchmark your actual workload at your actual batch size; 'GPU = faster' is true only when the math dominates the movement.

pitfalls: Putting every workload on GPU by default — transfer overhead makes small jobs slower
Renting the biggest GPU before profiling — utilization under 30% means money burned
Ignoring data loading — the GPU starves while the CPU struggles to feed it
lessons.try_it: Benchmark one of your models on CPU vs GPU at three batch sizes; note where the crossover is.

lessons.title: VRAM: The Real Constraint
concepts: VRAM (GPU memory) is the binding constraint in deep learning: models, activations, gradients, and optimizer state must all fit simultaneously
Rough sizing: parameters x bytes-per-param x 4 (weights + gradients + optimizer states) — a 7B model in fp16 needs ~7Bx2x4 = 56GB before activations
Batch size is the VRAM dial: halve the batch when you hit out-of-memory, and use gradient accumulation to keep the effective batch size
Activations scale with sequence length and batch: long-context inference eats VRAM far beyond the model weights

example.code:
# 7B param model, fp16 (2 bytes/param)
weights = 7e9 * 2          # 14 GB
grads   = 7e9 * 2          # 14 GB
optim   = 7e9 * 2 * 2      # 28 GB (Adam keeps 2 states)
# total ~56 GB + activations -> needs 80GB GPU or sharding
example.walkthrough: Adam stores two extra numbers per parameter (momentum and variance), so training memory is roughly 4x the weight size in fp16 — the 7B model needs ~56GB before a single activation is stored. This is why training needs far bigger GPUs than inference, and why the arithmetic above should precede every hardware decision.

pitfalls: Sizing by parameter count alone — forgetting gradients, optimizer states, and activations
OOM surprises mid-training — estimate before launching, not after the crash
Maxing batch size 'because it fits' — no headroom for activation spikes on long sequences
lessons.try_it: Estimate training VRAM for a 1B-parameter model in fp16 with Adam; which GPU tier fits?

lessons.title: Mixed Precision Training
concepts: Mixed precision trains in fp16/bf16 while keeping a fp32 master copy of weights: ~2x faster and half the memory with minimal accuracy loss
bf16 (brain float) is the safer choice on modern GPUs: same exponent range as fp32, so far fewer overflow/underflow headaches than fp16
Loss scaling counteracts fp16's tiny range: gradients are scaled up before the backward pass and unscaled after, preventing underflow to zero
Not all ops tolerate low precision: keep loss computation and reductions in fp32 — frameworks' autocast handles this automatically

example.code:
# PyTorch autocast pattern
with torch.autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    outputs = model(inputs)      # matmuls in bf16: fast, lean
    loss = criterion(outputs, y) # autocast keeps this stable
scaler.scale(loss).backward()    # loss scaling for fp16 safety
example.walkthrough: Autocast runs the heavy matmuls in bf16 (fast, half the memory) while keeping numerically sensitive ops in fp32 automatically. The gradient scaler multiplies the loss before backprop so tiny gradients do not underflow fp16's limited range, then unscales before the optimizer step. Net effect: near-fp32 accuracy at roughly twice the training speed.

pitfalls: fp16 without loss scaling — gradients silently underflow to zero and the model stops learning
Assuming 'precision = quality' — bf16 training matches fp32 on the vast majority of workloads
Mixed precision on old GPUs without tensor cores — no speedup, just complexity
lessons.try_it: Enable autocast on a training script and compare step time and final accuracy vs fp32.

lessons.title: Feeding the Beast: Data Loading
concepts: A starving GPU is the most common waste in ML: if data loading cannot keep up, thousand-dollar GPUs idle at 20% utilization
Dedicated loader workers (num_workers=4-8) preprocess batches on CPU in parallel while the GPU trains — overlap, do not serialize
Pinned memory and prefetching move the next batch to GPU while the current one computes, hiding transfer latency
Profile the pipeline first: if GPU utilization is low and CPU is pegged, the fix is data loading, not a bigger GPU

example.code:
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
loader = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=64, num_workers=8,
                      pin_memory=True, prefetch_factor=4)
# 8 CPU workers decode/transform; GPU never waits
example.walkthrough: Eight worker processes decode images and apply transforms on CPU while the GPU trains on the current batch; pinned memory plus prefetching stages the next batches for fast GPU transfer. The pattern is a pipeline: disk → CPU workers → GPU, all stages busy simultaneously. When GPU utilization jumps from 25% to 90% after this change, you just doubled your effective hardware for free.

pitfalls: num_workers=0 (default) — the GPU waits on a single Python process doing I/O
Heavy augmentation on the fly without workers — CPU becomes the bottleneck
Buying a second GPU when the first is starved — two idle GPUs cost twice as much
lessons.try_it: Check your training GPU utilization; if under 60%, tune num_workers and prefetching first.

lessons.title: Multi-GPU and Distributed Concepts
concepts: Data parallel is the standard pattern: each GPU holds a full model copy, processes a different data shard, and gradients are averaged across GPUs
Gradient synchronization (all-reduce) is the communication cost: fast interconnects matter more than raw FLOPS at scale
Effective batch size multiplies by GPU count — scale the learning rate with it (linear scaling rule, roughly)
Model parallel (splitting the model itself across GPUs) is for models too big for one GPU — complexity jumps an order of magnitude

example.code:
# data-parallel sketch: 4 GPUs
# per-GPU batch 32 -> effective batch 128
# each GPU: forward/backward on its shard
# all-reduce: average gradients across GPUs
# each GPU: optimizer step with averaged gradients
example.walkthrough: Four GPUs each process 32 examples, compute gradients locally, then all-reduce averages those gradients so every GPU applies the identical update — mathematically equivalent to one GPU with batch 128, but 4x the throughput. The learning rate typically scales up with the effective batch. All-reduce over slow networking kills the speedup, which is why interconnect bandwidth decides real multi-GPU performance.

pitfalls: Expecting 4 GPUs = 4x speedup with slow interconnect — communication eats the gain
Keeping the single-GPU learning rate at 4x batch size — training destabilizes
Reaching for model parallel before trying data parallel — 10x the complexity for problems data parallel solves
lessons.try_it: Compute your effective batch size across GPUs and check whether your learning rate scaled with it.

lessons.title: What to Log: Params, Metrics, Artifacts
concepts: Log the full configuration: hyperparameters, seeds, code version, and dataset hash — a result without its config is trivia
Log metrics at every meaningful granularity: per-epoch during training, final aggregates at the end — curves diagnose, numbers summarize
Log artifacts: the trained model file, preprocessing objects, and evaluation plots — everything needed to reproduce the result from the log alone
Name runs meaningfully (baseline-lr1e3, +dropout-0.3): future-you greps run names, not timestamps

example.code:
# minimal experiment log (JSONL, one run per line)
run = {'name': 'baseline-lr1e3', 'lr': 1e-3, 'seed': 42,
       'data_sha': '9f2c...', 'val_f1': 0.83, 'model_path': 'm_v3.pkl'}
open('runs.jsonl', 'a').write(json.dumps(run) + '\n')
example.walkthrough: One JSON line per run captures everything needed to interpret the result later: what was tried (lr, seed), on what data (data_sha), what happened (val_f1), and where the artifact lives (model_path). This 5-line pattern beats no tracking entirely — and it is the gateway habit to full tracking platforms later.

pitfalls: Logging metrics without params — you know the score but not what produced it
Timestamp-only run names — unsearchable archaeology within a month
No dataset hash — the result floats free of the data that made it
lessons.try_it: Start a runs.jsonl for your current project and log your next 3 runs in this schema.

lessons.title: Comparing Runs Fairly
concepts: Compare runs on identical evaluation data: different validation splits make score differences meaningless
Change one variable between runs: lr 1e-3 vs 3e-3 isolates the learning rate; changing lr, batch, and architecture teaches nothing
Track the delta, not just the absolute: '+0.02 F1 over baseline-lr1e3' is the unit of progress
Beware the multiple-comparisons trap: trying 50 configs and celebrating the best overstates the true gain — hold out a final test set

example.code:
# comparison discipline
baseline = get_run('baseline-lr1e3')          # val_f1 0.83
candidate = get_run('lr3e3')                  # val_f1 0.85
# same data_sha? same val split? one variable changed?
delta = candidate['val_f1'] - baseline['val_f1']  # +0.02, real or noise?
example.walkthrough: The comparison is only valid if both runs share the dataset hash and validation split and differ in exactly one variable. A +0.02 delta on a 500-example validation set might be noise — check with a second seed before declaring victory. This discipline turns a pile of runs into an actual search instead of a lottery.

pitfalls: Comparing scores across different validation splits — apples to oranges
Changing three things per run — no attribution when something improves
Declaring victory on noise — small deltas need replication
lessons.try_it: Pick your two best recent runs and verify they are comparable by these rules.

lessons.title: Reproducibility: Code, Data, Environment
concepts: Reproducibility has three legs: code version (git hash), data version (dataset hash), environment (pinned dependencies) — lose any one and the result cannot be replayed
Seeds are the fourth leg: log every seed, because unseeded runs are unrepeatable by definition
The reproduction test: hand your log to a colleague — if they cannot reproduce the number, your tracking is incomplete
Snapshot aggressively: disk is cheap, unrepeatable results are expensive

example.code:
# reproducibility checklist per run
# [ ] git rev-parse HEAD -> a3f9c1d
# [ ] dataset sha256    -> 9f2c...
# [ ] pip freeze        -> requirements-run42.txt
# [ ] seeds             -> 42 (python, numpy, torch)
example.walkthrough: Four lines in the run log — commit hash, data hash, frozen requirements, seeds — make any result replayable months later. When a reviewer, teammate, or future-you asks 'how did you get 0.91?', the answer is a lookup, not an excavation. Teams that do this debug in minutes what others debug in weeks.

pitfalls: Two of the four legs logged — reproducibility needs all four
'Latest main' as the code version — main moves; the hash does not
Seeds logged but data unhashed — replaying on different data proves nothing
lessons.try_it: Run the reproduction test: can you replay your best run from its log alone?

lessons.title: The Model Registry: Staging to Production
concepts: A model registry versions trained models like code: v1, v2, v3 with metadata, lineage, and lifecycle stages (staging, production, archived)
Promotion is gated: a candidate moves staging → production only by beating the champion on the holdout set plus passing latency and fairness checks
Champion/challenger: the production model (champion) keeps serving while the challenger proves itself — no unproven model takes 100% traffic
Every production model must answer: which code, which data, which metrics earned it this slot — the registry is that answer

example.code:
# promotion gate (pseudo)
if challenger.holdout_f1 > champion.holdout_f1 + 0.005 \
   and challenger.p99_ms < 200 and challenger.fairness_ok:
    registry.promote(challenger, stage='production')  # champion -> archived
example.walkthrough: The gate is explicit and automatic: the challenger must beat the champion by a margin (not noise), meet the latency SLO, and pass fairness checks before promotion. The registry records who promoted what, when, and why — so the 3 AM 'which model is live and why' question has a one-line answer.

pitfalls: Manual model swaps with no gate — hope as a deployment strategy
No champion/challenger — every new model takes 100% traffic on day one
Registry without lineage — versions without provenance are just filenames
lessons.try_it: Define the promotion gate (metric, margin, checks) for one of your models.

lessons.title: Experiment Culture: Notes and Decisions
concepts: The run log captures what happened; lab notes capture why: hypotheses, surprises, and decisions — write the reasoning, not just the numbers
A decision log entry: 'Chose dropout 0.3 over 0.5: val F1 equal, train gap smaller, simpler' — six months later this is gold
Review weekly: 30 minutes scanning recent runs surfaces patterns (all high-LR runs diverge) that daily tunnel vision misses
Share the log: a team-visible experiment history prevents three people from running the same failed idea

example.code:
# decision log entry
DECISION 2026-10-08: keep max_depth=8 over 12
WHY: val F1 0.851 vs 0.849 (noise), gap 0.03 vs 0.11
NEXT: try min_samples_leaf sweep before adding features
example.walkthrough: The entry records the decision, the evidence, and the next step in three lines. When someone proposes max_depth=12 next quarter, the log answers instantly. Weekly reviews compound this: patterns across runs surface only in aggregate, and the shared log turns solo trial-and-error into team knowledge.

pitfalls: Numbers without narrative — the log says what, nobody remembers why
No weekly review — insights rot in the log unexamined
Private notebooks — the team reruns your dead ends
lessons.try_it: Write decision-log entries for your last three modeling decisions.

lessons.title: Cleaning: Missing Data and Duplicates
concepts: Audit before you clean: isna().sum() and duplicated().sum() quantify the problem — cleaning without measuring is guessing
Missingness has types: MCAR (random), MAR (predictable from other columns), MNAR (missing because of the value itself) — the type constrains the fix
Median imputation is the robust default for numerics; mode for categoricals; model-based imputation when missingness is heavy and structured
Duplicates inflate metrics and leak across splits: dedupe BEFORE splitting, or the same row lands in train and test

example.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')
print(df.isna().sum().sort_values(ascending=False).head())
print('dupes:', df.duplicated().sum())
df = df.drop_duplicates()  # BEFORE any split
med = df['income'].median()
df['income'] = df['income'].fillna(med)
example.walkthrough: The audit sorts missingness so the worst columns surface first; duplicates are counted and dropped before any split (critical — dedupe after splitting leaks identical rows across the boundary). Income gets median imputation, robust to the outliers income columns always have. The order matters: dedupe, then split, then impute using train-only statistics.

pitfalls: Imputing with the mean on skewed data — outliers drag it away from typical values
Deduping after the split — identical rows in train and test inflate scores
Dropping all rows with any missing value — on wide data this can delete most of the dataset
lessons.try_it: Audit a real dataset: report the top-3 missing columns and the duplicate count.

lessons.title: Encoding Categorical Variables
concepts: One-hot encoding turns categories into binary columns: simple and safe, but explodes dimensionality on high-cardinality features
Ordinal encoding assigns integers (small=0, medium=1, large=2): only valid when the order is real — never for nominal categories like colors
Target encoding replaces categories with the mean target value: powerful for high-cardinality, but must be computed inside cross-validation folds to avoid leakage
Rare categories need handling: group into 'other' below a frequency threshold, or the model memorizes noise

example.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
enc = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore', sparse_output=False)
X_cat = enc.fit_transform(df[['city']])  # fit on TRAIN only
# high-cardinality alternative: df['city'] = df['city'].where(df['city'].map(freq) > 50, 'other')
example.walkthrough: One-hot with handle_unknown='ignore' survives new cities at serving time instead of crashing. The frequency-threshold line collapses rare cities into 'other' before encoding, taming dimensionality. Both fit on training data only — the encoder learned on train transforms validation and serving identically, which is the whole anti-leakage discipline in one line.

pitfalls: Ordinal-encoding nominal categories — the model invents an order (red < blue) that does not exist
Target encoding on the full dataset — the target leaks into the features
One-hot on a 10,000-value ID column — dimensionality explosion and a model that memorizes
lessons.try_it: Encode one categorical column two ways (one-hot vs frequency-thresholded) and compare dimensions.

lessons.title: Scaling and Normalization
concepts: Scaling matters for distance- and gradient-based models (kNN, SVM, neural nets, regularized regression) — features on different scales distort them
StandardScaler (zero mean, unit variance) is the default; MinMaxScaler (0-1 range) when bounds matter; RobustScaler when outliers dominate
Tree models do not need scaling — splits are threshold-based and scale-invariant, so skip it and save the complexity
Fit scalers on training data only: the scaler's mean/variance are training statistics, and test data must never contribute to them

example.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_s = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)  # learn mean/var HERE
X_val_s = scaler.transform(X_val)          # apply, never refit
X_test_s = scaler.transform(X_test)
example.walkthrough: fit_transform learns the mean and variance from training data alone; transform applies those frozen statistics to validation and test. Refitting on validation would let validation statistics shape the training representation — subtle leakage. For trees, skip all of this: the splits do not care whether income is in dollars or thousands.

pitfalls: Scaling before the split — test statistics leak into training through the scaler
Scaling for tree models — harmless but pointless complexity
MinMaxScaler with extreme outliers — one outlier compresses everything else into a sliver
lessons.try_it: Check your current project: was the scaler fit on train only? Fix it if not.

lessons.title: Target Leakage: The Silent Killer
concepts: Target leakage is information from the future or the label smuggled into features: the model scores brilliantly and fails in production
Classic sources: features computed after the outcome (cancellation reason predicting cancellation), IDs that encode the label, aggregates including the target row
The smell test: if a feature feels 'too predictive', investigate — legitimate features rarely give 0.99 AUC on hard problems
The cure is temporal discipline: every feature must be computable from information available at prediction time, using only past data

example.code:
# leakage audit questions per feature:
# 1. Could I compute this at prediction time? (no future data)
# 2. Does it derive from the label or its consequences?
# 3. Would it exist for a brand-new, unseen example?
# Any 'no' -> drop or rebuild the feature
example.walkthrough: Run every feature through the three questions. 'Days since last login' passes: computable at prediction time from past events. 'Refund issued' for predicting churn fails question 2 — it is a consequence of the outcome, available only after the fact. Leakage audits feel paranoid until the first time they save a production launch.

pitfalls: 'The model will figure out what's useful' — it figures out the leak, not the problem
Aggregates over the full history including the target period — future data in disguise
Skipping the audit because CV scores look great — great scores are the symptom
lessons.try_it: Audit your top-5 features by importance with the three leakage questions.

lessons.title: Text and Date Features
concepts: Dates are feature mines: extract year, month, day-of-week, hour, days-since-event — raw timestamps are nearly useless to models
Cyclical features need circular encoding: hour 23 and hour 0 are adjacent — sin/cos transforms preserve that (hour_sin, hour_cos)
Text basics: length, exclamation counts, and TF-IDF vectors capture surprising signal before any embedding model
Beware future-dated fields: 'last_updated' timestamps after the prediction point are leakage wearing a timestamp costume

example.code:
df['hour'] = df['timestamp'].dt.hour
df['hour_sin'] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df['hour'] / 24)
df['hour_cos'] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df['hour'] / 24)
df['dow'] = df['timestamp'].dt.dayofweek  # Mon=0..Sun=6
df['title_len'] = df['title'].str.len()
example.walkthrough: Hour becomes two circular features so the model sees 23:00 and 00:00 as neighbors instead of opposites — a linear model on raw hour cannot learn that midnight wraps around. Day-of-week captures weekly seasonality; title length is a cheap text signal. Each extraction is deterministic and leakage-free as long as the timestamp precedes the prediction point.

pitfalls: Raw timestamps as features — the model cannot use '2026-10-04 13:22:01' directly
Linear hour encoding — midnight becomes maximally distant from 11 PM
Using updated_at instead of created_at — the update happened after the outcome
lessons.try_it: Extract 5 date features and 2 text features from a real dataset you have.

lessons.title: Data Drift vs Concept Drift
concepts: Data drift: the input distribution shifts (customers get younger) while the input-output relationship holds — the model sees unfamiliar territory
Concept drift: the relationship itself changes (what 'fraud' looks like evolves) — the model's learned mapping goes stale even on familiar inputs
The distinction drives the fix: data drift may need retraining on new data; concept drift needs re-examining labels and features
Detect drift statistically: PSI (Population Stability Index) and KS tests compare production feature distributions against the training baseline

example.code:
# PSI rule of thumb
# PSI < 0.1: no significant shift
# 0.1-0.25: moderate shift, investigate
# > 0.25: significant shift, act
# track per-feature PSI weekly vs training baseline
example.walkthrough: PSI bins a feature's training distribution and production distribution and measures the divergence: under 0.1 the world looks familiar; over 0.25 something structurally changed. Track it per feature weekly. When age's PSI jumps to 0.4 after a marketing campaign targets students, that is data drift — the inputs moved. When fraud patterns mutate and chargeback labels shift meaning, that is concept drift — the mapping moved.

pitfalls: Treating all drift as 'retrain more' — concept drift needs new labels, not just new rows
No training baseline stored — drift is unmeasurable without something to compare against
Monitoring only predictions — input drift is invisible until damage is done
lessons.try_it: Pick your top-3 features and define how you would detect drift in each.

lessons.title: Monitoring Without Ground Truth
concepts: Production labels arrive late or never (fraud confirmed weeks later; churn observed months later) — you cannot wait for accuracy
Proxy metrics fill the gap: prediction distribution shifts, confidence/entropy changes, and business KPIs correlated with model quality
Prediction drift is the early warning: if the output distribution moves while inputs look stable, suspect the model or the world changed
Delayed-label evaluation: when labels do arrive, score the predictions made weeks ago — maintain the join between predictions and eventual outcomes

example.code:
# prediction log schema (enables delayed eval)
{'request_id': r, 'model_v': 'v4', 'features_hash': h,
 'pred': 0.83, 'ts': t}
# weeks later: join with labels on request_id -> true accuracy
example.walkthrough: Every prediction is logged with a request ID, model version, and timestamp. When fraud labels arrive three weeks later, joining on request_id reconstructs the true accuracy of predictions made weeks ago — the only honest production metric. Meanwhile, a sudden shift in the prediction distribution (mean fraud score jumping from 0.2 to 0.5) pages you long before labels confirm it.

pitfalls: Waiting for labels to monitor — by the time accuracy is measurable, the damage is booked
No prediction logging — delayed evaluation is impossible without the join key
Monitoring inputs but not outputs — the model's behavior is the thing you ship
lessons.try_it: Design the prediction log schema for one of your models, including the delayed-label join.

lessons.title: Alerting Without Alert Fatigue
concepts: Alert on symptoms that need action: sustained accuracy drop, feature PSI breach, prediction distribution shift — not every wobble
Thresholds need hysteresis and cooldowns: alert when PSI > 0.25 for 2 consecutive checks, then suppress for 24h — flapping alerts get ignored
Severity tiers: page for 'model down/wildly wrong', ticket for 'drift detected, investigate this week' — not everything is a page
Every alert must name the action: 'age PSI 0.4 — check marketing campaign targeting' beats 'drift detected'

example.code:
# alert rule sketch
if psi['age'] > 0.25 and consecutive_breaches >= 2:
    ticket('Data drift: age PSI=0.4, likely campaign shift. Action: verify, consider retrain.')
    cooldown(24h)  # no repeat pages while investigating
example.walkthrough: The rule requires two consecutive breaches (killing single-sample noise), files a ticket rather than paging (drift is investigate-this-week, not wake-someone), names the suspected cause and the action, and cools down for 24 hours so the on-call is not spammed while investigating. Alerts that cry wolf train humans to ignore them — then the real failure pages into silence.

pitfalls: Alerting on every threshold twitch — fatigue guarantees the real alert gets missed
No severity tiers — drift and downtime page identically, so both get ignored
Alerts without actions — 'something is wrong somewhere' helps nobody
lessons.try_it: Write one alert rule (condition, severity, action, cooldown) for a model you own.

lessons.title: Retraining Triggers and Strategies
concepts: Scheduled retraining (weekly/monthly) is the baseline: simple, predictable, and sufficient when drift is gradual
Trigger-based retraining fires on evidence: PSI breach, accuracy drop on delayed labels, or data volume thresholds — retrain because something changed
Full retraining vs fine-tuning: full rebuilds on all data are simplest and most robust; fine-tuning is cheaper but risks catastrophic forgetting
Always champion/challenger the retrained model: the new model must beat the current one on recent holdout data before promotion — retraining is not automatically an upgrade

example.code:
# retraining policy
schedule: weekly full retrain on rolling 12 months
triggers: psi_breach(any feature) or delayed_acc_drop(>3pts)
gate: challenger must beat champion on last-30d holdout by +0.005
example.walkthrough: The policy combines a weekly cadence (predictable, catches gradual drift) with event triggers (catches sudden shifts), and the promotion gate ensures retraining only ships actual improvements. A retrained model that scores worse on recent data stays in staging — 'fresh' is not the same as 'better', and the gate is what enforces that.

pitfalls: Retraining on a schedule but never checking if the new model is better — freshness theater
Trigger-only retraining with no baseline schedule — slow drift accumulates unnoticed
Auto-promoting every retrain — some retrains are worse, and now they are live
lessons.try_it: Write the retraining policy (schedule, triggers, gate) for one production model.

lessons.title: Feedback Loops: When Models Eat Their Own Outputs
concepts: Feedback loops form when model predictions influence future training data: the fraud model's blocks change which fraud gets observed, biasing the next training set
The signature: performance looks stable or improving while real-world effectiveness decays — the model is grading its own homework
Mitigations: holdout regions never exposed to the model, exploration traffic (small random decisions), and external ground truth that bypasses the loop
Log the decision context, not just the outcome: what the model saw, what it decided, and what would have happened otherwise (counterfactuals where possible)

example.code:
# loop example: content recommendation
# model promotes X -> users click X (it's shown) -> clicks train next model
# result: model 'learns' X is best because it showed X most
# fix: 5% exploration traffic shown randomly, logged separately
example.walkthrough: The recommender shows X because the model ranked it first; users click X because it is shown; the clicks train the next model to rank X first. The loop is self-reinforcing and invisible in offline metrics. Exploration traffic — a small slice of random or epsilon-greedy decisions, logged separately — breaks the loop by observing what the model would not have chosen.

pitfalls: Training on model-influenced outcomes as if they were natural — the loop compounds silently
No exploration traffic — the system can never learn what it never tries
Judging looped systems by their own metrics — the ruler is bent
lessons.try_it: Identify one feedback loop risk in a system you know and sketch the mitigation.

lessons.title: Containerizing Models
concepts: A container packages model, code, and dependencies into one immutable unit: it runs identically on your laptop and in production
Pin everything in the image: base image tag, Python version, requirements with hashes — 'latest' is how deployments break on rebuild
Keep images lean: multi-stage builds and slim bases shrink a 3GB image toward 500MB, speeding deploys and scaling
The model artifact belongs in the image or mounted from versioned storage at startup — never baked in unversioned or fetched from 'the folder'

example.code:
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY api.py model_v4.pkl ./
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "api:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0"]
example.walkthrough: The Dockerfile starts from a pinned slim base, installs pinned requirements without cache bloat, copies the API code and the versioned model artifact, and launches the server. Rebuilding this image anywhere produces the identical runtime — the 'works on my machine' class of incident disappears. The model file's version (v4) is explicit: swapping models means building a new image, which is reviewable and rollback-safe.

pitfalls: FROM python:latest — unpinned bases make rebuilds non-reproducible
Model fetched from a shared folder at runtime — unversioned, unaudited, un-rollbackable
Bloated images with build tools left in — slow deploys, bigger attack surface
lessons.try_it: Write a Dockerfile for one of your model APIs with pinned versions throughout.

lessons.title: CI/CD for Machine Learning
concepts: ML CI has two tiers: fast tests (unit tests, schema checks, lint — minutes) run on every commit; slow tests (training smoke runs, eval gates — hours) run on schedule or merge
Test the data, not just the code: schema validation, null-rate bounds, and distribution checks catch the corrupt-data commits that break training
The eval gate is ML's unique CI step: the candidate model must beat the baseline on holdout before merge — code that trains a worse model fails the build
CD for ML deploys the pipeline, not just the model: versioned artifacts flow staging → canary → production with automated gates

example.code:
# ci.yaml sketch
fast: [lint, unit-tests, schema-check]      # every commit, <10 min
slow: [train-smoke-1pct-data, eval-gate]  # nightly + pre-merge
# eval-gate: challenger F1 >= champion F1 - 0.002 or FAIL
example.walkthrough: Fast tests guard every commit in minutes; slow tests (a 1%-data training smoke plus the eval gate) run nightly and before merges. The eval gate is the key ML addition: a commit whose model regresses beyond tolerance fails CI like a broken unit test. CD then promotes the passing artifacts through staging and canary automatically.

pitfalls: Running full training in per-commit CI — hour-long builds that everyone bypasses
No data tests — a corrupt CSV breaks the nightly train and nobody knows until morning
CD that ships code but hand-copies models — half the system bypasses the pipeline
lessons.try_it: Split your ML CI into fast/slow tiers and add one data test this week.

lessons.title: Deployment Strategies for Models
concepts: Blue-green: v4 (blue) serves while v5 (green) warms up beside it — flip the router when green is healthy, flip back in seconds if not
Canary: route 5% of traffic to v5, compare live metrics (error rate, p99, business KPI), then ramp 5 → 25 → 50 → 100%
Shadow: v5 scores live traffic but its answers are discarded — pure observation with zero user impact, ideal for risky changes
Choose by risk: routine retrain → canary; architecture change → shadow then canary; emergency fix → blue-green for instant rollback

example.code:
# canary ramp plan
phase1: 5%  for 30min  -> check error_rate, p99, KPI
phase2: 25% for 2h    -> compare vs baseline
phase3: 100%          -> promote; keep v4 warm 24h
# any phase fails -> route back to v4 (seconds)
example.walkthrough: The canary ramps in measured phases with explicit checks at each step; v4 stays warm for 24 hours so rollback is a routing change, not a redeploy. Shadow mode would precede this for a risky architecture change. The strategy is chosen by risk level, not habit — and every strategy keeps the previous version one flip away.

pitfalls: Big-bang 100% swaps — maximum blast radius for every release
Canary without metric comparison — traffic ramps but nobody checks the numbers
Deleting the old version immediately — rollback becomes a rebuild
lessons.try_it: Write the canary ramp plan (percentages, durations, checks) for your next model release.

lessons.title: Cost and Resource Planning
concepts: GPU cost dominates ML budgets: an idle GPU burns the same dollars as a busy one — autoscale to zero for batch/dev, right-size for serving
Separate cost tiers: training (spot/preemptible where possible), batch inference (scheduled spot), online serving (reserved/steady)
Track cost per prediction: total serving spend divided by predictions — the metric that makes optimization tradeoffs concrete
FinOps for ML: tag resources by project/model, alert on spend anomalies, and review the top-3 cost drivers monthly

example.code:
# cost intuition (illustrative)
# online serving: 2 GPUs x 24h x $3/hr = $144/day steady
# batch nightly: 4 GPUs x 2h x $1/hr spot = $8/day
# same predictions, 18x cost difference -> match mode to need
example.walkthrough: The arithmetic is stark: steady online GPUs cost $144/day while a nightly spot batch does equivalent work for $8. This is why the batch-vs-online decision from the serving domain is also a financial decision. Cost-per-prediction turns abstract bills into an optimizable number — halve it and you have funded your next experiment.

pitfalls: Online serving for batchable work — the single most expensive ML anti-pattern
No spend alerts — the $12k surprise bill arrives monthly
Training on on-demand when spot would do — 3x the necessary training cost
lessons.try_it: Compute cost-per-prediction for one of your serving setups this week.

lessons.title: ML Incident Response
concepts: ML incidents differ from software incidents: the system is 'up' but wrong — bad predictions, drifted inputs, or a poisoned retrain
First response is containment via routing: shift traffic back to the previous model version while you diagnose — rollback first, root-cause second
The incident kit: prediction logs (what did it output?), feature PSI (did inputs shift?), recent deploys/retrains (what changed?), eval history
Post-incident, harden the gate that should have caught it: eval thresholds, drift alerts, or data validation — incidents are gate failures

example.code:
# ML incident runbook (first 15 min)
1. Route 100% traffic to previous model version (seconds)
2. Freeze retraining pipeline (stop the bleeding)
3. Pull: prediction logs, PSI dashboard, deploy/retrain history
4. Diagnose from evidence; write the timeline as you go
example.walkthrough: Routing back first restores correct behavior in seconds while diagnosis proceeds without user impact — the ML equivalent of failing over. Freezing retraining prevents a poisoned pipeline from shipping a second bad model mid-incident. The timeline written during the incident becomes the post-mortem's backbone, and the post-mortem's job is naming which gate failed and how it gets fixed.

pitfalls: Debugging for an hour while bad predictions serve — containment before diagnosis
No prediction logs — the incident is undiagnosable after the fact
Post-mortem blames the data scientist — the gate failed, not the person
lessons.try_it: Draft the first-15-minutes runbook for a 'model is wrong' incident on your system.

lessons.title: Capstone: End-to-End ML Service — Overview
concepts: Your capstone: a production-style ML service: data pipeline, trained model, tracked experiments, served API, container, and monitoring
Break the build into phases: plan, build, secure, validate, document. Each phase maps to domains in this bootcamp
Document as you go — your write-up is the interview artifact that proves senior-level ownership
Done beats perfect: a working system with honest limitations beats an unfinished ambitious one

example.code:
Phase 1: Design the service: data flow, model choice, API contract, and deployment topology
Phase 2: Build the training pipeline with versioned data and tracked experiments
Phase 3: Serve the model behind a validated API with health checks and versioning
Phase 4: Containerize, define the canary release plan, and wire up drift monitoring
example.walkthrough: Treat each phase as a mini-project with a definition of done. Demo each phase working before moving on — integration surprises compound.

pitfalls: Starting to build before writing the plan — an hour of planning saves ten of rework
Skipping documentation until the end — you will forget why decisions were made
Gold-plating phase one while phase four remains untouched
lessons.try_it: Write the one-paragraph project plan: what you will build, in what phases, and what 'done' looks like.

lessons.title: Capstone: Validation and Demo
concepts: Validate every requirement with a test you can show: screenshots, command output, or a live demo
Prepare the 5-minute demo narrative: problem, approach, build, validation, lessons learned
Anticipate questions: know the trade-offs you made and what you would do with more time
Publish the write-up: architecture diagram, build log, validation evidence, reflection

  1. The problem (30s)
  2. Architecture overview (60s)
  3. Live walkthrough (2 min)
  4. Validation evidence (60s)

Hiding limitations — name them before you are asked
No architecture diagram — draw the system before you demo it

lessons.title: AI Lab Orientation: What You Will Build
concepts: This bootcamp builds you into someone who ships ML systems, not just trains models: data pipelines, experiment discipline, serving, and monitoring
The arc: Python foundations -> pipelines -> training -> serving -> retrieval -> compute -> tracking -> deployment, then the capstone ties it together
Every domain ends in the terminal: the labs are where concepts become skills — reading without doing does not count here
Your capstone is the interview artifact: an end-to-end ML service you can demo, explain, and defend

Reading lessons without running the labs — the terminal is where learning sticks
Treating the mock as a study tool — it is a measuring tool; study first, measure after
