lessons.title: The AI Stack: From Data to Deployed Model
concepts: The modern AI stack has layers: data -> features -> training -> registry -> serving -> monitoring — each layer has its own failure modes
Data is the foundation: most production ML failures are data failures (drift, leakage, corruption), not modeling failures
The registry is the hinge between training and serving: versioned, gated, and attributable — or your deployments are folk art
Monitoring closes the loop: production behavior feeds back into retraining decisions, making the stack a cycle rather than a pipeline

example.code:
data (versioned) -> pipeline (validated) -> training (tracked)
  -> registry (gated) -> serving (monitored) -> retraining (triggered)
Each arrow is a contract; each contract is testable.
example.walkthrough: When something breaks in production, walk the stack bottom-up: is the data right? Did the pipeline validate? Which model version is live? What do the monitors say? This walk is the incident response skeleton for every ML system you will ever operate.

pitfalls: Blaming the model for data problems — check the foundation first
No registry — training and serving connected by hope and filenames
Open-loop deployments — no monitoring means no learning from production
lessons.try_it: Draw the stack for a system you know and mark which layers have contracts and which run on hope.

lessons.title: Reading ML Documentation Like an Engineer
concepts: Docs answer three questions: what does it do, what are its inputs/outputs, what are the failure modes — read for all three
API references beat tutorials for precision: tutorials show the happy path; references document the edge cases you will actually hit
Version-pin your reading: docs for v2.3 describe v2.3 — the function signature you memorized may have changed
Reproduce the example before trusting it: run the docs' snippet, then mutate one parameter to test your understanding

example.code:
Doc-reading protocol:
  1. Skim for the mental model (what is this thing?)
  2. Read the API signature (exact inputs, outputs, defaults)
  3. Hunt the failure modes (raises? NaN? OOM?)
  4. Run the example; break it once on purpose
example.walkthrough: The fourth step is the differentiator: deliberately breaking the example (wrong shape, missing arg, huge batch) teaches the failure modes faster than any tutorial. Engineers who read this way debug in minutes; engineers who skim debug for days.

pitfalls: Tutorial-only learning — the happy path teaches nothing about failures
Reading docs for the wrong version — signature mismatch confusion
Never running the examples — unexecuted knowledge evaporates
lessons.try_it: Pick one library you use, run its flagship example, then break it three ways and note each error.

lessons.title: Responsible AI: Safety Basics for Builders
concepts: You are responsible for what you ship: biased training data becomes biased decisions at scale — audit datasets and outputs for disparate impact
Test for failure, not just success: adversarial inputs, edge populations, and distribution shift belong in your eval suite
Privacy is architectural: minimize data collection, hash or drop PII early, and know your retention obligations before you log everything
Document limitations honestly: every model card should state what the model cannot do — the limitation section is a safety feature

example.code:
Pre-ship safety checklist:
  [ ] Evaluated on edge populations, not just the majority
  [ ] Adversarial / noisy inputs tested
  [ ] PII handling reviewed; retention defined
  [ ] Limitations written down where users will see them
example.walkthrough: The checklist takes an hour and catches the issues that become incidents: the model that fails on a dialect, the log full of SSNs, the silent limitation nobody disclosed. Safety is not a separate phase — it is a property of how you build every phase.

pitfalls: 'The data is what it is' — data choices are design choices with consequences
Safety as a launch-week scramble — untestable that late
Hidden limitations — users cannot work around limits they cannot see
lessons.try_it: Run the safety checklist against one model or project you have built.

lessons.title: Debugging ML Code: Shapes, NaNs, and Silent Bugs
concepts: Shape mismatches are the most common ML bug: assert tensor shapes at function boundaries — print debugging shapes beats staring at code
NaNs propagate silently: one NaN in the data becomes NaN loss becomes NaN weights — check inputs for NaN/inf before blaming the model
Silent bugs are worse than crashes: a shuffled label column trains happily to garbage — validate data invariants, not just code correctness
Bisect ruthlessly: half the pipeline, test, repeat — the bug is where the invariant breaks, and bisection finds it in log(n) steps

example.code:
import numpy as np
assert X.shape == (n_samples, n_features), X.shape
assert np.isfinite(X).all(), 'NaN/inf in features'
assert set(np.unique(y)) <= {0, 1}, 'unexpected labels'
# three lines that catch 80% of data bugs before training
example.walkthrough: These assertions at the pipeline entrance catch the bugs that waste GPU hours: wrong shapes from a bad merge, NaNs from a corrupt column, labels from a misaligned join. Run them on every dataset load — they cost milliseconds and save days. When training misbehaves, bisect: check data, then preprocessing output, then model — the break is always at one boundary.

pitfalls: Debugging the model before validating the data — the data is guilty far more often
No shape assertions — silent broadcasting bugs train on wrong-shaped tensors
Ignoring the first NaN — it never stays contained
lessons.try_it: Add the three assertion lines to your data loading code and run them on your current dataset.

lessons.title: Testing ML Pipelines: Data Tests and Contracts
concepts: Data tests are unit tests for datasets: schema checks (columns, types), range checks (age 0-120), and null-rate bounds run on every pipeline input
Pipeline contracts declare stage guarantees: 'transform outputs no nulls, same row count' — violations fail fast with the stage named
Golden datasets: a small fixed input with known-good output that the pipeline must reproduce exactly — your regression test for the whole DAG
Test at the boundaries: the most valuable tests sit between stages, catching the handoff bugs that stage-local tests miss

example.code:
# data contract test (runs at ingest)
assert set(df.columns) == EXPECTED_COLS
assert df['age'].between(0, 120).all()
assert df.isna().mean().max() < 0.2, 'null rate exploded'
assert len(df) > 1000, 'suspiciously small batch'
example.walkthrough: These four assertions at ingest catch the corrupt upstream export, the schema change nobody announced, and the partial-day file — before training burns hours on garbage. The golden dataset goes further: run the full pipeline on 100 fixed rows and diff against the known-good output; any diff is a regression with the stage identified by the contract checks.

pitfalls: Testing code but not data — the pipeline is correct and the input is garbage
No golden dataset — regressions surface as mysterious metric drift
Contracts only at ingest — handoff bugs between stages go uncaught
lessons.try_it: Write data contract tests for one pipeline input you own.

lessons.title: Transfer Learning and Pretrained Models
concepts: Transfer learning reuses models trained on massive datasets: take a pretrained backbone, replace the head, fine-tune on your (small) data
The recipe: freeze the backbone, train only the new head first (fast, stable), then unfreeze the top layers with a small learning rate
It works because early layers learn general features (edges, textures, grammar) that transfer across tasks — you only teach the task-specific top
Watch for domain mismatch: a model pretrained on natural images transfers poorly to X-rays — the further the domain, the more you must fine-tune

example.code:
# fine-tuning recipe
backbone = load_pretrained('resnet50'); freeze(backbone)
model = attach_head(backbone, n_classes=YOUR_CLASSES)
train(model.head, lr=1e-3)            # stage 1: head only
unfreeze(backbone.top_layers); train(model, lr=1e-5)  # stage 2: gentle
example.walkthrough: Stage 1 trains only the new head with the backbone frozen — fast and stable, since the pretrained features are already good. Stage 2 unfreezes the top layers with a tiny learning rate so task-specific features adapt without destroying the pretrained knowledge (catastrophic forgetting). Ten times less data than training from scratch, often better accuracy.

pitfalls: Fine-tuning everything at high LR immediately — destroys pretrained weights on day one
Freezing forever — leaves task-specific gains on the table
Ignoring domain mismatch — pretraining on the wrong domain transfers the wrong features
lessons.try_it: Fine-tune a pretrained model on a small dataset using the two-stage recipe.

cheatsheet: Model = folder: weights + tokenizer + config. Product = everything around it.
Quantization exchange rate: 16-bit → 8-bit → 4-bit halves memory each step; fidelity cost is the price.
Runtime tiers: llama.cpp/Ollama (runtime) → LM Studio/Jan (desktop) → Open WebUI (browser) → vLLM (production serving, operators only).
Agent loop: request → agent → memory → tools → runtime → eval → retry → deploy.
Main-writer / silent-advisor: separate the roles; review at plan approval, stuck errors, pre-commit.
Evals prove the agent passed the evals. Always ask what the eval would miss.
Open weights ≠ open source. Local ≠ private. Bigger model ≠ fixed product.

simulations.title: The silently drifting recommender
simulations.brief: Click-through rate on the recommendation widget fell 18% over two weeks. No errors in the serving logs, latency is flat, and the model was never redeployed. Something upstream changed.

steps.symptom: CTR down 18% over 14 days, no serving errors, no deploys.
evidence: p99 latency 41ms (unchanged), error rate 0.02% (unchanged), model version churn-v2.3 (unchanged since March)
user_age_days: 100% of live values are > 400 days old — the feature-sync job has been failing silently for 13 days
Model trained when user_age_days had mean 96 days; production now sees mean 812 days
options: Fix the feature-sync job and backfill user_age_days, then retrain the model on fresh features
Scale the serving fleet to 3x replicas to handle the load
Raise the ranking score threshold from 0.5 to 0.8 to filter weak recommendations
Roll back to churn-v2.2 — the previous model cannot be worse than this
steps.explain: The model is fine; its input is stale. The feature-sync job died 13 days ago, so the model scores with training-time features — classic train/serve skew. Replicas and thresholds treat the symptom. Repairing the pipeline and retraining on fresh features fixes the cause.

simulations.debrief: Most 'model' regressions are data regressions. When metrics decay with no deploy and no errors, check feature freshness first: compare live feature distributions against what the model trained on. Train/serve skew is the default suspect.

simulations.title: Eval says green, users say broken
simulations.brief: The offline eval suite is green — 94% pass rate — but support tickets about the assistant's answers tripled this month. The eval is lying about something.

steps.symptom: Eval green (94%), support tickets 3x, no changes to the model weights.
evidence: 2,400 prompts collected in 2022; the set was last refreshed 14 months ago
v7 shipped 3 weeks ago: adds a tools block and a system reminder the model never saw in eval
Pins prompt template v4 — the eval runs a template users have not seen in months
options: Refresh the eval set with recent production traffic and pin the harness to the live template v7
Add 500 more 2022-era prompts to the eval set to increase coverage
Lower the eval pass threshold to 85% so the suite matches user sentiment
Blame the ticket spike on seasonality and close the investigation
steps.explain: The eval measures the wrong thing: stale prompts through a stale template. Evals must track production — same template, fresh traffic samples — or their green light is fiction.

simulations.debrief: An eval is a contract with production. Refresh eval sets from recent traffic, version the prompt template in the harness, and treat 'green eval, angry users' as an eval bug until proven otherwise.

simulations.title: Pick the serving stack
simulations.brief: The churn model must score 40M users nightly and serve 2,000 live requests per second at p99 under 100ms. Choose the serving design.

steps.text: Nightly batch scoring of 40M users plus a live 2,000 rps path. Serving design?

choices.label: Batch-score the 40M users on the warehouse at night; serve the live path with a small distilled model on GPUs behind autoscaling
choices.feedback: Correct: batch the bulk work where it is cheap, serve the live path with a small fast model. The 32B model never touches the hot path.

choices.label: Score all 40M users live through the 32B model on demand
choices.feedback: A 32B model at 2,000 rps with p99 under 100ms is a cost and latency disaster. Batch what is batchable; distill what must be live.

simulations.debrief: Serving is an economics problem: batch the predictable, distill the interactive, and never pay real-time prices for work that can wait until night.

simulations.title: Triage the model incident
simulations.brief: The fraud model started approving obvious fraud at 3 AM. Put the triage steps in the right order.

items: Inspect live feature distributions vs training
Check data pipeline freshness and schema
Freeze the rollout / route traffic to the stable version
Compare canary vs stable on the fraud recall metric

simulations.debrief: Stop the bleeding first (freeze the rollout), then diagnose data before model, compare against the stable version, and only then decide the fix. Debugging a model that is still serving bad decisions costs money every minute.

simulations.title: Review the serving config
simulations.brief: This inference service config is headed to production. Click the misconfigured lines (2 issues to find).

steps.config:
model: churn-v2.3
replicas: 2
request_timeout_ms: null
gpu_memory_fraction: 0.95
max_batch_size: 64
fallback_model: none
eval_hook: enabled

issues.description: No request timeout — one hung request ties up a worker forever and cascades across replicas.
issues.fix: Set request_timeout_ms to a bounded value (e.g. 2000).

issues.description: No fallback model — if v2.3 fails, the service fails hard instead of degrading to the previous version or a rules baseline.
issues.fix: Configure fallback_model to the last stable version.

simulations.debrief: Production inference needs guardrails the notebook never had: timeouts so one bad request cannot wedge the fleet, and a fallback so a model failure degrades gracefully instead of failing hard.
